rules.full_text:
26
Travel in Morzomotha
OVERVIEW
Morzomotha is a lightless 
system of caves and tunnels 
far below the surface of the 
world. Vast cathedral caves 
are as common as cramped, 
claustrophobic tunnels. 
Lightless rivers surge through 
prehistoric caverns, and even a 
black and cursed ocean crashes 
within Morzomotha's belly. 
The beings who dwell here are 
utterly alien to the surface, and 
their ways of life are anathema 
to sunborn creatures.
CLIMATE
In the depths of the earth, there 
are neither seasons nor weather. 
Instead, these deep tunnels 
are humid and cool year round, 
never changing in a way that 
drives creatures of the sun mad. 
When the season changes on 
the surface, PCs in Morzomotha 
must pass DC 12 CHA checks or 
take 1d4 CHA damage.
THE CHITTERING
Charisma damage does not heal 
as normal in Morzomotha. A 
character must be bathed in full 
sunlight for their CHA damage 
to begin healing. 
When a PC goes below 6 
CHA, The Chittering sets in. 
Their teeth begin to chatter 
uncontrollably, and they emit a 
thin, high-pitched whine that 
draws the Shadowdark's worst 
denizens like sharks to blood. 
PCs can suppress the outward 
effects of The Chittering for 1d4 
rounds with a successful DC 12 
CON check.
Characters who reach 0 CHA in 
Morzomotha go irrevocably mad.

1403. MEDUSA DEN
Odd clusters of stalagmites are 
actually petrified humanoids 
and beasts that have been 
artfully posed by Kalithia, a 
medusa. She specializes in 
depicting the moment of terror 
before a violent death. Kalithia 
is practical and lucid; she might 
part with her Staff of the Cobra 
(SD pg. 317) in exchange for rare 
creatures or bodies to petrify.
1404. THE CLAWS
In a forgotten corner of the 
tunnel, the statue of a black, 
crouching figure cradles a book 
to its chest. This is the legendary 
Tome Mordanticus (SD pg. 
318); touching it or the statue 
teleports the group to hex 709.
1507. LIBRARY OF LENG
A spired castle of glistening, 
green-black stone rises high 
over a moat-like ravine. Deep 
carvings of titanic, winged 
horrors cover its walls. Here, the 
ghoulish Librarians of Leng 
greedily collect rare tomes and 
forbidden lore. The librarians 
study and document the fears of 
all living beings, and they value 
this knowledge highest of all.
1510. ANCIENT ALTAR
A shallow, circular amphitheater 
plunges into the stone floor of 
this cave. At its center, a round 
altar of rune-carved malachite 
has been cracked in two. Anyone 
who approaches it hears a 
whispered voice in Primordial: 
"Return our names. Return our 
power." Placing the books from 
hex 207 and 1404 on the altar 
releases a subsonic pulse felt by 
all beings. The two Lost deities 
regain their True Names and a 
shred of their former strength; 
their return has begun, and the 
world starts to remember them.
1601. MAUGRINHOLD
A squat fortress of crude stone 
blocks. 30 duergar slavers lair 
here, but their leader has been 
mentally dominated by an 
imperious magical sword named 
Ivernicaste, Eternal Winter. The 
duergar are now the sword's 
fearful playthings. Ivernicaste 
is a chaotic +2 greatsword that 
deals 2d10 damage and seeks 
a worthy wielder. It has +7 CHA 
and tries daily to dominate a 
wielder it deems weak. Once a 
month, it can turn into an ice-
rimed archdevil for 10 rounds.

rules.full_text:

THE LIBRARY OF LENG
The Library of Leng is a castle of green-black rock that stretches 
into windowless, pointed spires as if shaped from clay. High-relief 
carvings of colossal figures spring out of its walls, each as tall as 
the castle itself. They depict tentacled and winged horrors locked 
in mortal combat with thrashing dragons. The entire structure sits 
heavily on a pillar of stone surrounded by a 200'-deep ravine. A thin, 
arching bridge dripping with strands of fungi crosses this expanse; 
it deposits visitors at a tunnel mouth leading into the castle's base.
ORDER OF BATTLE
Intelligent creatures (excluding sentient books) in adjacent rooms 
investigate unusual sounds, arriving in 1d4 rounds. A Librarian of 
Leng whose morale breaks retreats toward Area 52 to release the 
bezelak. If it succeeds, all random encounters have a 3:6 chance of 
being with the bezelak for the next day. During this time, checks 
to sneak and hide are DC 18 and encounters with the Librarians of 
Leng or their servants are always hostile.
ENTRANCES AND EXITS
Area 1. A bridge crosses over the ravine and into a tunnel mouth at 
the base of the Library. This tunnel leads to Area 1.
Area 12. An overflow grate in the cistern (Area 12) covers a chute 
that exits the pillar of rock 60 feet below the Library. Crusted lichen 
and white, chalky minerals surround the mouth of it. PCs can climb 
between it and the bridge to Area 1 with two DC 15 STR/DEX checks. 
Area 15. A wagon-sized carving of a beast with 10 snaking eyestalks 
and a crescent moon maw (The Ten-Eyed Oracle) lurks at the rear 
side of the Library above a narrow precipice of rock. It seems out of 
proportion to the rest of the gigantic figures surrounding it. A secret 
door built into this beast's scarred central eye opens to Area 15.

Dozens of books are  skewered on them; black ink runs down the fangs like blood.   • Fangs. Execution site for condemned sentient books. Skewering  a sentient book here grant
rules.full_text:

5. THE FANGS
Humid cave that smells of rotting paper pulp. Six ivory, curving 
fangs as tall as men thrust from the floor. Dozens of books are 
skewered on them; black ink runs down the fangs like blood.  
• Fangs. Execution site for condemned sentient books. Skewering 
a sentient book here grants 3 XP but deals 1d4 CHA damage.
• Books. Most are dead. Four still flap weakly and whisper for 
mercy. Removing a living book from a fang allows it to heal.
 ▶ "They Walk Among Us" (paranoid; believes 1 in every 20 people 
is a doppelganger), "In Sunlit Lands" (has gone mad; begs to be 
returned to the wizard's college in the City of Masks), "Memoirs 
of Malfune" (devious and sly; it details the life of the sorcerer 
Malfune the Traitor), "Bibliodemon Biology" (clinical; it analyzes 
the Librarian of Lengs' painfully acute senses).
6. CAVE CRABS
The entire rear wall churns with a carpet of hand-sized, gray crabs. 
The cave hisses softly with thousands of tiny claws tapping on stone.  
• Crabs. 200 soft-shelled crabs interlock their legs and slurp up 
cave minerals. Treat as 3 piranha swarms. Delicious to eat raw. DC 
12 STR to pull one free; cumulative 1:20 chance to provoke attack.
 ▶ Skeleton. The crabs cover a deep one skeleton wearing Bracers 
of Defense (SD pg. 301) engraved with suckered squid tentacles.
7. HUNGRY FROST TROLL
A lanky, ice-encrusted giant lunges and gnashes wildly at the end of 
a chain cuffed around its neck. The chain groans and strains.
• Giant. Underfed frost troll named Hrog. It breaks its weakened 
chain in 1d4 rounds after smelling nearby prey.
 ▶ Hungry. Giving the troll fresh meat calms its rage. It speaks 
Giant haltingly and says it will be good if freed (it won't). It fears 
the whips of the "fish-men" and wants to slaughter them.

10. CISTERN ENTRANCE
Four screw-threaded pillars sweat beads of water that trickle down 
and stream along the gently sloping floor toward the north.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Pillars. They turn like screws. Tightening all four intensifies the 
steam in Area 11, causing the brain eaters to run out yelping.
11. SAUNA
Hissing gills along the floor disgorge gouts of white steam. Human-
sized shapes move within the pale cloud.
• Shapes. Two visiting brain eaters scholars, Talurac (stern, soft-
spoken) and Graalix (arrogant, bold). Not immediately hostile. 
They can hear the PCs' surface thoughts. They want to steal "The 
Hexagonal Tome" from Area 42 and are willing to cut a deal.
 ▶ Treasure. Talurac's delicate Wraith Chain (SD pg. 321) is folded 
neatly on a bench. Graalix wears a Necklace of Charm (SD pg. 
308) fashioned from shark teeth.
12. CISTERN
A humid, dripping room of gray-green stone. Every surface is slick 
with moisture. The floor slopes toward a lightless hole in the center.
• Slick. Aggressive movement requires DC 12 DEX not to slip on the 
floor and fall. Creatures who do slide into the hole.
• Stingbats. After two rounds of noise in Area 12, six stingbats fly 
out of the hole (see below) and attack interlopers.
• Hole. 10' deep. Leads to cave-like cistern, same size as room above 
with waist-deep water and a grate on the wall at neck height.
 ▶ Stingbats. Six stingbats hang upside down from the ceiling.
 ▶ Grate. DC 18 STR to pry off. Opens to a sharply angled chute (big 
enough for a human) that drops overflow water 140' down into 
the ravine outside (see Area 12 in Entrances and Exits, pg. 39).

Large enough for creatures to pass  through. The other side is 10,000 years in the past.  ▶ Cumulative 1:6 chance per

13. TIME TEAR
Bright green light flashes around a jagged oval on the back wall of 
the cave. It looks out onto sunlit grassland blowing in the wind.
• Oval. A tear in space-time. Large enough for creatures to pass 
through. The other side is 10,000 years in the past.
 ▶ Cumulative 1:6 chance per round a group of 2d6 prehistoric, 
spear-wielding beastmen  and their 1d4 trained smilodons walk 
by. They approach the oval with fear and puzzlement.
14. GLASS GATE
A drafty cave with a portcullis at its east end. The bars are a green, 
translucent material bristling with barbs. Past the portcullis, the air 
shimmers like a mirage.
• Portcullis. DC 20 STR to lift. Barbs deliver a toxin; DC 15 CON or 
scream "Intruder!" in Primordial for 1d4 rounds. Lever is in Area 15. 
• Mirage. Teleports creatures who walk through it to Area 29. 
15. GLASS LEVER
An enclosed cave with green, translucent lever protruding from the 
wall. Hooked barbs sprout from its handle.
• Lever. Opens/closes the portcullis in Area 14. Barbs deliver a toxin; 
DC 15 CON or scream "Intruder!" in Primordial for 1d4 rounds.
• Secret Door. In the south alcove wall. It exits to an outdoor 
precipice behind the Library (see Entrances and Exits, pg. 39).
16. FLOATING EYES
About a dozen apple-sized, floating orbs dart around the cave.
• Orbs. 10 in total. Each is an eye with a snake-like pupil and neon-
colored iris. DC 15 DEX each round inside room to avoid colliding 
with one. Touching an eye hits the target with a random eyestalk 
ray effect of The Ten-Eyed Oracle (see SD pg. 255), but 1:6 chance 
of imparting a one-time use of the effect to the target instead.

17. PILLARS OF PETRIFICATION
Thick iron chains hang from two rows of stone pillars. A human  with 
a long beard is lashed to one, his face contorted in silent agony. 
• Pillars. The pillars slowly and painfully petrify any humanoid 
lashed to them into a gargoyle over the course of 1d4 hours. 
Gargoyles lose the memory of their former lives.
• Human. Finnius Dexitorus (L mage), captured after he teleported 
here by accident. He's half-petrified and has lost most of his 
memories. Kind-hearted, but also horrified and confused.
18. KITCHEN
Two fish-faced men in white aprons charge around a kitchen full of 
roiling pots and fire-belching ovens. It smells of steamed crab.
• Men. Cooking deep ones, Lork (head chef, militant) and Flarb 
(sous chef, loyal). They don't look up when the door opens. Lork 
yells, "You're late, moron! Get to work!" and tosses an apron. 
 ▶ Knife. Lork's butcher knife is a +2 vorpal dagger (beheads a 
humanoid opponent on a natural 20 attack roll).
19. ALCHEMY ROOM
A nine-foot tall figure in purple robes stoops over a table cluttered 
with bowls and vials. Wall racks and work table hold countless 
varieties of colorful bottles. The sharp reek of alcohol fills the air.
• Figure. A Librarian of Leng named Riarn. He's brewing a potion. 
DC 15 DEX to approach him stealthily. He is furious at being 
interrupted. He has a master key to all locked areas. 
• Bottles. Alchemical ingredients. Eye-watering liquids, chalky 
powders, clumpy balls of fungus, neon-colored gels. Mixing at 
least three ingredients together has a 2:6 chance of producing a 
random magic potion (SD pg. 282 and 286). Otherwise, it creates 
a noxious gas (DC 15 CON or 1d6 CON damage to all within near).
 ▶ Potions. A Potion of Forgetfulness (SD pg. 310) sits on the table.

It guards the  potions and poisons from unauthorized access. The contingency  to end its servitude is by speaking its True
rules.full_text:

20. ELIXIR STORAGE
Several bottles cluster on storage shelves along the walls.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Guardian. An invisible stalker hides along the wall. It guards the 
potions and poisons from unauthorized access. The contingency 
to end its servitude is by speaking its True Name.  
• Shelves. Labeled in Primordial as "Potions," "Poisons," and "Inks."
 ▶ Potions. A Potion of Giant Strength, Potion of Polymorph, and 
Potion of Vitality (SD pg. 310-311).
 ▶ Poisons. 4 vials (1 dose each) of Vapor of Leng, an oily yellow 
gas that works when inhaled. DC 15 CON or INT stat becomes 3 
for 1d4 hours and subject experiences terrifying hallucinations.
 ▶ Inks. 1 bottle of Magic Ink (SD pg. 306), 1 bottle of Purple Ink 
(see Area 59), 1 bottle of gold-flecked ink (worth 200 gp).
21. HALL OF MIRRORS
Ten-foot tall mirrors stand in the alcoves, each set into a heavy 
frame of a sculpted metal.
• Mirrors. Frames are adorned with cavorting satyrs and devils.
 ▶ Gold. Northern alcove. Magically enhances the viewer's beauty 
(+1 CHA stat for a day, limit 1/week). 
 ▶ Silver. Central alcove. Actually a Mirror of Mischief (SD pg. 307). 
Evil duplicates immediately try to blow the PCs' cover.
 ▶ Meteorite. Southern alcove. Magically improves the viewer's 
intellect (+1 INT stat for a day, limit 1/week).
22. ROBING ROOM
Wall hooks hold extremely long, silky robes and yellow sashes.
• Robes. 6 complete outfits the Librarians of Leng wear (robes and 
the sashes they use to cover their eyes and ears). Sized for 9-foot 
tall beings. The robes are morzo moth silk and each worth 100 gp.

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf

26. BACKWARDS MOTION ROOM
The surfaces in this room subtly bend and move when not directly 
observed, creating an uneasy sense of vertigo.
• Movement.  Moving toward any destination in this room while 
facing it causes it to grow more distant at an equal speed (it 
extends into an infinite dimensional rupture). Walking backwards 
toward the destination mitigates this effect.
27. ALTAR OF TERROR
Two rows of inky black pillars stand before an alcove housing a dark 
altar. A human woman in rags lies upon it, unmoving. 
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Pillars. Touching a pillar allows one to view the nightmares of the 
victim on the altar (see below) as if through their eyes.
• Altar. Oily black marble placed on an ornamental red carpet. A 
creature lain upon the altar enters an endless nightmare (DC 15 
CHA to resist) until it is removed. 
 ▶ Carpet. A Flying Carpet (SD pg. 303). The weighty altar requires 
a DC 20 STR check to lift for long enough to pull it free. 
• Woman. A powerful young witch, Anamaxis (C archmage). Proud 
and cold. She is currently without spells and suffering from 
extreme deprivation. Her priority is escaping the Library of Leng.
28. EYE OF DEATH
Patches of black powder are sprinkled on the floor. The northeast 
wall has a broad, oval-shaped carving at it center. 
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Powder. Smells of charred meat (it's disintegrated bodies).
• Carving. A closed eye. It opens when any creature in the 
room speaks in a language other than Primordial. It shoots a 
disintegration ray at the offender (DC 15 DEX or 5d8 damage).

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf

Areas 31 and 56 overlook the hall through  hidden arrow slits (can be found by actively looking). A Librarian  of Leng watche
rules.full_text:
52
30. JADE HALL
A vast, silent hall reaches up and out into endless darkness. Jade 
floor tiles flare with a reflective glow as light washes over them. 
• Hidden Watchposts. Areas 31 and 56 overlook the hall through 
hidden arrow slits (can be found by actively looking). A Librarian 
of Leng watches from inside each. 
 ▶ Hostile. Librarians immediately attack any creatures outlined in 
the green aura from the door trap in Area 29.
• Lever. On the wall outside the door to Area 52. It opens and closes 
the grate covering the pit in Area 52.
31. HIDDEN WATCHPOST
A tall, purple-skinned being in red robes presses its silk-wrapped 
face up against arrow slits lining the walls. It sniffs at the air.
• Being. A Librarian of Leng monitors Area 30 through arrow slits 
hidden from the outside.
 ▶ Hostile. Librarian immediately attacks any creatures outlined in 
the green aura from the door trap in Area 29.
• Secret Door. To Area 33.
32. FORTUNE-TELLER
A goblin in a silk turban sits on a pillow inside a tall glass cube on a 
red base. Dazzling lights along the glass flash in wavelike patterns.
• Goblin. The Great Zambini, a mechanical goblin. He tells a fortune 
with strobing eyes and a robotic voice when 1 gp is inserted into 
a vertical slot in the cube's base. Anyone who inserts more than 5 
gp a day: DC 15 CON check or struck deaf and blind for one day.
 ▶ Fortunes. Roll 1d6. 1: Misfortune. A random item you carry 
disappears forever. 2: Woe. Lose 1d6 XP. 3: Unclear. Lose a luck 
token. 4: Promising. Gain a luck token. 5: Weal. Gain 1d4 XP. 6: 
Good fortune. A weapon you carry gains a permanent +1 bonus.

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf

Light  can't fully banish the shadows that spread like pools of oil. • Ceiling. Stretches infinitely up with row after row of statuettes. • St
rules.full_text:

42. BOOKS OF PRIMORDIALS
Black, bent statuettes of winged and tentacled abominations crowd 
the wall shelves. The ceiling extends up and up into darkness. Light 
can't fully banish the shadows that spread like pools of oil.
• Ceiling. Stretches infinitely up with row after row of statuettes.
• Statuettes. Dull black stone, 2 feet high, each a different 
primordial being. Every statuette holds the book that describes 
the members of its species. Finding a specific book takes 3 hours 
and requires flight (a Librarian of Leng can locate it immediately).
 ▶ "The Hexagonal Tome." Held by the brain eater statuette. The 
visiting brain eaters in Area 11 want to steal it.
 ▶ "Servants of the Eye." Held by the Librarian of Leng statuette. 
Every Librarian of Leng instantly becomes aware if someone 
touches the book. They savagely pursue anyone who does so.
43. THE BOOK OF IMMORTALS
An infinitely black room that echoes cavernously. A beam of light in 
the far distance pours down onto a marble plinth holding a book.
• Book. An ordinary, brown leather tome titled "That Which 
Is." Each chapter is infinite in length and describes a unique 
immortal being. It can't be removed from its plinth.
 ▶ Reading. A mortal who reads passages about their god or 
patron gains a patron boon or class talent (once only). Reading 
about an immortal whose alignment does not match the 
reader's requires a DC 15 CHA check or the reader goes mad.
44. SILENT READING ROOM
Oversized, plush armchairs cluster around the edges of the room.  
• Armchairs. All sound is muted for anyone sitting in one.
 ▶ Book. "An Analysis of Mirror Demons," left open on the seat of 
an armchair. Contains a Spell Scroll of Mirror Image.

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf

DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open. • Trap. A hair-thin tripwire crosses each threshold to the north,  west, and south, causing a h
rules.full_text:

45. TROLL TRAINING GEAR
Wall racks hold coiled black whips, iron neck collars big enough for 
bears, and iron chains. A lever protrudes from the northeast wall.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Trap. A hair-thin tripwire crosses each threshold to the north, 
west, and south, causing a hidden bucket of caustic acid (3d6 
damage) to fall on anyone in the threshold (DC 15 DEX to avoid).  
• Racks. One hook cradles a +2 whip called Backbiter. 1/day, on a 
missed attack with it, turn the miss into a critical hit instead. Any 
frost troll that sees Backbiter must make a morale check.
 ▶ Whip. Melee weapon, near range, 1d4 damage, finesse property.
• Lever. Ordinary iron. Operates gate leading into Area 29.
46. FROST TROLL CAVE
Four rangy giants with warty blue skin and black eyes pace 
restlessly at the end of thick chains bolted around their necks.  
• Giants. 4 frost troll captives. They whine, plead, and threaten 
to be released in broken Giant. Trolls: Sibolg (ringleader), Erdak 
(aggressive), Mulda (devious), Bral (cowardly). 
 ▶ Neck Chains. 10' long, bolted to wall. DC 20 STR to break. Freed 
trolls betray all agreements and run to Area 47 to massacre the 
trainer. Then they go on a wild rampage. Random encounters 
have a 3:6 chance of being with the trolls until they are killed. 
47. TROLL TRAINER
A rotund, fish-faced man sits at a low table and gobbles a steaming 
plate of crab with both hands, flinging bits of it everywhere.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Man. Troll trainer. A flatulent and overconfident deep one named 
Urghast. Feels other deep ones are beneath him and would like 
to see them "put in their place." Has a key to Areas 45 and 47.

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf
rules.snippet: 58 48. MESS HALL Two fish-faced men sit alone at tables and shovel plates of food into  their slobbering, fanged mouths. They shoot glares at each other. • Men. Two deep ones, Borbin (hot-headed, sarcastic) and Mulko  (irritable, greedy). Each believes the other cheated on a recent  dice game. A sho
rules.full_text:

48. MESS HALL
Two fish-faced men sit alone at tables and shovel plates of food into 
their slobbering, fanged mouths. They shoot glares at each other.
• Men. Two deep ones, Borbin (hot-headed, sarcastic) and Mulko 
(irritable, greedy). Each believes the other cheated on a recent 
dice game. A shouting match erupts between them in 2 rounds, 
and a fist fight 2 rounds after that.
 ▶ Rematch. Both would agree to a rematch to settle the dispute.
 ▶ Treasure. Mulko quaffs a stolen Potion of Giant Strength before 
pummeling Borbin. Otherwise, he tries to pawn it off to the PCs. 
49. DEEP ONES QUARTERS
Shallow pools of lapping water pockmark the floor. Human-like 
shapes float inside them. The smell of fish is overwhelming.
• Pools. Waist-deep, the size of a human bed. 6 deep ones float on 
them face-down, asleep. DC 12 DEX to sneak by them unnoticed.
 ▶ Treasure. A sleeping deep one wears a waterlogged Bag of 
Holding (SD pg. 299) on his belt filled with 300 pounds of 
slightly off fish. DC 15 DEX to pluck it free without waking him. 
• Key. A master key to all locked areas hangs by the east door.
50. MASSACRE CAVE
Piles of bones and dried gore carpet the cave floor in a sticky mess. 
Heavy snuffling and scraping echoes from the north.
• Bezelak. For each loud noise, cumulative 1:6 chance the bezelak 
in Area 51 comes to investigate. 
• Treasure. A gold and ruby glint on a mangled skeleton's hand is a 
Ring of Fireballs (SD pg. 312). 
• Bars. Heavy iron. Blocks the west passage. DC 20 STR to lift.
• Secret Door. In the rock pillar. It opens to a slippery, corkscrewing 
tunnel that climbs 60' (DC 18 DEX to climb) and exits into Area 8.

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf
rules.snippet: 59 51. BEZELAK LAIR A broad cave tunnel. Black streaks of feces and blood paint every  surface. Overhead, a square shaft reaches up to a distant grate. The  eye-watering stench of algae and sulfur boils thickly in the air.  • Bezelak. Clings to the wall 20' up, camouflaged by the muck- spattered sto
rules.full_text:
59
51. BEZELAK LAIR
A broad cave tunnel. Black streaks of feces and blood paint every 
surface. Overhead, a square shaft reaches up to a distant grate. The 
eye-watering stench of algae and sulfur boils thickly in the air. 
• Bezelak. Clings to the wall 20' up, camouflaged by the muck-
spattered stone (it gets a surprise round if unnoticed). It's very 
hungry and does not discriminate between friend or foe.
• Shaft. 40' high. Covered in a heavy grate. Leads to Area 52.
52. DROP PIT
A narrow walkway surrounds a grate-covered pit dropping into 
darkness. The reek of sulfur and stagnant water wafts through it.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Pit. Covered in a grate (lever to withdraw it is outside door in Area 
30). The bezelak in Area 51 can swiftly climb the pit's 40' walls.
53. OBSERVATION CAVE
A high platform thrusts out over a dripping cave strewn with bones.
• Platform. 40' high, leads to Area 54. The underside is greased 
regularly with tallow (pg. 22), making it too slippery to climb.
• Man. A gap-toothed old man (peasant) who calls himself Prince 
Rork lurks in the shadows. He wears stitched-together skins 
and alternates between a tittering stream-of-consciousness and 
wheezing laughter. The bezelak (Area 51) refuses to eat him. 
 ▶ Caw. If in danger, he screeches a hawk-like caw, instantly 
summoning the bezelak from Area 51.
 ▶ Treasure. He wears hidden stacks of jewelry under his tunic and 
trades them for food. 1. Hefty gold and mithral braid (200 gp), 
2. Gold snake cuff with emerald eyes, as Bracers of Archery (SD 
pg. 301) 3. White gold chain with cat-eye ruby (250 gp), 4. Silver 
and pearl torc (150 gp), 5. Half-moon sapphire pendant (300 gp).

rules.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf

Each time entering, DC 15 INT or perceive the room to be  filled with salt water. "Swim" at half speed. Can actually drown. 58. ELITE GUARDS Two men

57. WATER ILLUSION
Translucent green water fills this room from top to bottom, cutting 
off abruptly at the open threshold to the east. 
• Illusion. Each time entering, DC 15 INT or perceive the room to be 
filled with salt water. "Swim" at half speed. Can actually drown.
58. ELITE GUARDS
Two men in black, spiny plate armor and helms stand at attention. 
The southeast wall has a broad, oval-shaped carving at it center. 
• Men. Elite deep one guards (treat as reavers with the deep one's 
sunblind trait). Nobody except Librarians of Leng may pass; they 
demand explanations in Primordial.
• Carving. A closed eye. It opens when any creature in the 
room speaks in a language other than Primordial. It shoots a 
disintegration ray at the offender (DC 15 DEX or 5d8 damage). 
59. HEAD LIBRARIAN'S OFFICE
A towering being in purple robes with intricate gold trim sits at a 
desk and passes its fingers over the open page of a book, mouthing 
words to itself with a hideous grin.
• Locked Door. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Being. The head Librarian of Leng, Xenoxes. Ruthless, precise. 
Fascinated with the common fears of surface-dwellers, such as 
spiders, snakes, and darkness. Wishes to study these trends.
 ▶ Treasure. Has a master key to all locked areas and wears the 
Talisman of Leng, a mithral pendant with a clawed hand 
clutching a black pearl with a silver snake-eye pupil. Its wielder 
gains +2 AC and can summon The Ten-Eyed Oracle as an ally 
for 10 rounds once a month (the Oracle hates overuse of this).
• Desk. 3 vials of Purple Ink (each enough for a short sentence). Ink 
can alter entries in any of the books in Areas 33, 34, 38, 40, and 42. 
It does not work on the Books of Immortals in Area 43.

On the east wall, an oily green tome stands inside an alcove.   • Archway. Large enough for an elephant. Between the arches, a  surface of
rules.full_text:

60. COMMUNING CHAMBER
A monumental stone archway carved with gargoyles and a leering 
demon face fills the west wall. Moss and fungi spirals up its pillars. 
On the east wall, an oily green tome stands inside an alcove.  
• Archway. Large enough for an elephant. Between the arches, a 
surface of inky darkness ripples like water and absorbs all light.
 ▶ Surface. Touching it reveals a distant, silent image of The Ten-
Eyed Oracle. The Oracle turns and approaches the viewer, 
crossing through the archway into Area 60 in 1d4 rounds unless 
someone touches the surface again, deactivating the archway.
• Tome.  The Tome of Leng. Bound in basilisk skin. A snake-like 
eye rolls around on the cover. Each time a mortal being opens 
the book, they age 2d6 years. A random sorcerer spell (pg. 15) 
appears inside the book each time it's opened.
61. SCRIBING HALL
Four lavender-skinned, willowy beings with pained smiles hunch 
over writing desks and scratch black quills across parchment. 
• Beings. 4 Librarians of Leng named Cirroc (irritable), Medzel 
(overwhelmed), Jalash (languid), and Vireen (fussy).
• Desks. Carefully stacked piles of scribed parchment. Scattering 
the piles causes the Librarians to sink helplessly to their knees in 
mental agony for one round. 
62. BOOK BINDING HALL
Two silk-robed, purple beings with mocking grins carefully pull 
needles and thread through stacks of parchment. Partially bound 
books crowd the work tables.
• Beings. 2 Librarians of Leng named Darog (cool-headed) and 
Nuriok (gossipy).
• Books. The only complete tome is "The Red Spectacle," a tale of 
gladiatorial prowess (reader gains +1 to melee attacks, one use).

26
Downtime
PCs can do one downtime 
activity between adventures. 
Activities marked with an 
asterisk* cost 10 gp x PC level.  
To succeed on a downtime 
activity, a character must pass 
the associated check. PCs can't 
use luck tokens on these checks.
If a PC fails a check, reduce its 
DC one step the next time they 
attempt it (reset after success).
SPIRITUALISM
Meditation, prayer, self-
reflection, or mystical study.
WIS Check
• DC 9: Gain favor with a 
local church. Your renown 
increases by 1 point.
• DC 12: Spiritual strengthening. 
You gain 2 XP.
• DC 15*: Find personal insight. 
Reroll one prior talent roll. 
• DC 18*: Spiritual cleansing. 
End one curse afflicting you.
SKULDUGGERY
Thievery, criminal activity, or 
churning the rumor mill. 
CHA Check
• DC 9: Start a rumor about 
one person. Their renown 
increases or decreases by 1 
point (you choose).
• DC 12: Lay low. Escape the 
City Guard over a minor crime.
• DC 15: Extortion. Increase the 
value of your next sale by 25%, 
or reduce the cost of your 
next purchase by 25%. 
• DC 18: Hide out. Escape the 
City Guard over a major crime.
DEX Check
• DC 15*: Get away with a minor 
crime, such as petty theft. 
If you fail, the City Guard 
investigates (see pg. 45).
• DC 18*: Get away with a 
major crime, such as murder. 
If you fail, the City Guard 
investigates (see pg. 45).

rules.full_text:
45
Law and Order
BREAKING THE LAW
There are many ways to break 
the law in the City of Masks, but 
they all fall into two categories:
Minor Crime
• Murder of a commoner
• Petty theft (100 gp or less)
• Disruptive public behavior
• Minor blackmail or conspiracy 
Major Crime
• Murder of a merchant, noble, 
or City Guard member
• Arson, kidnapping, depravity
• Major theft (101 gp or more)
• Treason or major blackmail
GETTING CAUGHT
The City Guard pursues minor 
crimes for 1d4 days and major 
crimes for 3d4 days. PCs who 
have committed a crime have 
a 1:6 chance each day of being 
confronted for arrest by a 
retinue of City Guard. 
JUDGMENT
The Duke's 12 magistrates 
judge all but the most severe 
crimes. There is a 1:6 chance 
the PCs stand before a corrupt 
magistrate who accepts bribes. 
Defendants can argue their case 
and present witnesses. Then, 
they make a CHA check (DC set 
by GM). Hiring a barrister for 500 
gp grants ADV on the check.
PUNISHMENT
Failure on the check results in a 
conviction, usually the following:
Minor Crime
• Returning stolen goods
• Fines, lashings, or serving 
time in the stocks
• Short-term forced labor
Major Crime
• Public execution
• Life term in the Duke's Donjon
• Exile on pain of death

rules.full_text:
46
Holidays
The City of Masks is famous for 
its many festivals, balls, and 
masquerades. Residents view 
these celebrations as delightful 
times of romance and drama.
Elaborate masks and costumes 
are both status markers and 
ways to hide one's identity. 
Below are the major holidays 
(there are many smaller ones).
LASTMOON
A celebration of the last full 
moon of the year. Residents 
eat sugar plums and sip spiced 
wine. A marriage proposal on 
this night is auspicious. The 
Midnight Waltz is the high point 
of the evening's festivities.  
Carousing. Roll an extra benefit 
this night. There is a 1:20 chance 
of receiving a marriage proposal.
Garb. Silver and cool tones only. 
It is a faux pas to wear gold or 
the warm tones of summer (-1 to 
carousing event rolls).
MAYTIDE
When the canals run swift and 
clear with the spring runoff, 
Maytide has come. Celebrants 
eat marzipan cookies shaped 
into delicate flowers and drink 
sweet honey mead throughout 
a day of music and dance. Deals 
or ventures begun on Maytide 
will be blessed with wealthy 
results. Many foreign nobles 
and dignitaries travel to the city 
especially for this festival.  
Carousing. Gain +1 to carousing 
event rolls. Roll any benefits with 
a +15% bonus. 
Garb. Floral colors, peacock 
feathers, white roses, or corsages 
are a must (-1 to carousing 
event rolls if not wearing at 
least one). Revelers favor pearls, 
diamonds, and bright gems 
(wearing such jewelry with a 
total value of at least 200 gp 
grants +1 to carousing event 
rolls). Black cloth or dark jewel 
tones are utterly out of place (-1 
to carousing event rolls).

rules.full_text:
47
NIGHT OF ST. ANTON
A raucous autumn celebration 
of the knight who slayed a devil 
and saved the 12 fair maidens it 
was trying to kidnap. Revelers 
smoke meats over open flames, 
dance the frantic Devil's Leap, 
and act out the roles befitting 
their costumes. Mischief is at an 
all-time high this night.
Carousing. Roll an extra mishap 
this night, but gain +2 to 
carousing event rolls. 
Garb. Costumes and masks 
depicting horned devils, noble 
knights, or fair maidens. Crimson 
red, glittering gold, and silken 
white are the colors of choice. 
Dressing otherwise is -1 to 
carousing event rolls.  
THE DUKE'S BALL
In high summer, a fairy tale 
night of whimsy and elegance 
occurs. The Duke throws a 
gilded ball at Montmar Castle, 
and all citizens who are dressed 
gloriously may enter and revel 
with the high society. The Duke 
chooses one woman to dance 
with in the Duke's Waltz that 
night. It is the highest honor, 
though her mask prevents her 
identity from truly being known.
Carousing. Gain +2 to carousing 
event rolls. Roll benefits with 
advantage. There is a 1:20 chance 
the Duke invites a female PC to 
dance the Duke's Waltz.
Garb. The most luxurious 
costume and mask (required) 
one can afford. Gold, gems, 
pearls, silk, and lacework are all 
in high demand. If the costume's 
total value is at least 500 gp, 
the wearer can enter Montmar 
Castle. Gain +1 to carousing 
event rolls if the total value of 
the costume is 1,000 gp or more. 
The color red is utterly forbidden 
due to fearful superstition about 
the Rat Plague (-3 to carousing 
event rolls and risk of arrest).

Gedgarrin District
Class: Wealthy.
Category: University district.
City Guard Arrives: 1d6 rounds 
1. FLASHING STEEL
Mareniel Siruul, an elf from the 
far desert, teaches swordplay 
and archery in her sunlit training 
hall. She is a serene teacher 
who rarely speaks. Her elegant 
techniques have been gaining 
traction in the city, and rumors 
stir that rival school Tiborian's 
(24) is planning to attack the 
hall to put Mareniel to shame. 
Students have ADV on Martial 
Training downtime checks with 
finesse weapons and bows.
2. THE PALE TOAD
A squat, cottage-like tavern with 
a blue gout of smoke spewing 
merrily from its chimney. Its 
white timbers, twin staircase, 
and two firelit front windows 
give it the appearance of a toad 
at rest. Students and staff from 
Gedgarrin (4) land here on their 
rare trips outside the university's 
walls. A forlorn young wizard 
named Teomin often sits in 
a dark corner scribbling and 
crumpling up love letters to 
Cynthia Ulfric (23). He's willing 
to lend his alchemical expertise 
to sympathetic souls. INT 
spellcasters get a +1 bonus to 
carousing event rolls here.

rules.full_text:
51
3. MONVEAU THEATER
A small and beloved theater 
that showcases up-and-coming 
talent. The resident playwright, 
Bertrand Gilliard, is about to 
debut his magnum opus, "The 
Horror Within." Unknown to all, 
Bertrand's quest for inspiration 
drove him to wander the tunnels 
below the theater where he 
found an eldritch book that 
drove him mad. His new play is 
a ritual that will summon forth a 
horror from the outer darkness.   
4. GEDGARRIN
The seven austere, grey towers of 
this wizard college rise high over 
the river. Its wise, grey-robed 
headmaster, Ivanculus, is said 
to have been taught by dragons. 
The school's six professors guide 
students over the many years it 
takes to achieve true mastery. 
Professor Laudren Mallen, the 
school's meek scrying instructor, 
has secretly joined The Shroud 
(pg. 43) after they promised 
to install him as Gedgarrin's new 
headmaster. Once a month, 
those permitted to research at 
the university's vast library gain 
ADV on one Magical Research 
downtime check.
5. THE ROUND
A gilded theater supported by 
marble pillars carved as giants 
and dragons holding up a 
domed, starry roof. The Round 
is the grandest stage ever built 
and has hosted history's most 
famous bards. A disgraced 
singer named Robirook once 
disappeared down the flooded 
passages beneath the stage; 
some claim to see this lost 
virtuoso weeping in the rafters 
during stirring performances. 
Bards get a +1 bonus to 
carousing event rolls here.
6. BARDIC COLLEGE
A warm and sunlit bastion 
of academic prowess and 
enlightenment. Music and 
poetry fill its swooping halls, and 
young bards bustle between 
galleries where renowned tutors 
teach history, philosophy, and 
oration. Chancellor Yeothin, the 
college's Master Poet, leads the 
effort to protect and share these 
sacred arts. Yeothin is a close 
friend to the Duke, and he works 
tirelessly in secret to subvert The 
Shroud and its temptations of 
ill-begotten power. See pg. 42 
for more college details.

21. MONTMAR CASTLE
Crimson and gold banners fly 
over this shining hilltop castle 
of pale stone. The Duke's loyal 
knights (pg. 43) defend its 
heavily fortified walls. Inside 
the castle's palatial halls, 
marble pillars and stained glass 
windows reach high overhead. 
The Montmar family has spared 
no expense filling their redoubt 
with sumptuous paintings, 
tapestries, and sculptures. The 
castle's legendary ballroom 
is a thing of crystal and gold, 
swooping stairs and balconies. 
The Duke's secret service, the 
Onyx Eye, knows much of the 
castle's network of hidden doors 
and tunnels, including those 
that lead to the donjon (19).
22. THE GOLDEN MARMOT
The finest inn in the city with a 
gold statue of a fat marmot in 
the lobby. Important diplomats 
and merchants enjoy the inn's 
superb cuisine and lavish suites 
staffed by a personal butler and 
4 private guards (50 gp a night). 
The capable Chief Concierge, 
Emule Virdan, doesn't permit 
riffraff and knows all their tricks. 
Entry requires 8+ renown.
23. THE SILK LION
A family dynasty of tailors who 
serve the Montmar family itself. 
Cynthia Ulfric, talented but 
young, just inherited her late 
father's duties. She is secretly 
heartbroken that the endless 
work has robbed her of the 
time to pursue her love, the 
apprentice wizard Teomin 
studying at Gedgarrin (4). 
Cynthia is the only tailor in the 
city who can create incredible 
masquerade costumes of 500 gp 
value or more (each one takes a 
week). Her reputation requires 
that her clients have 8+ renown, 
but Cynthia makes exceptions 
for those who earn her trust 
(these clients must come after 
hours to avoid sparking gossip).
24. TIBORIAN'S
Tiborian, a surly, retired 
gladiator, teaches an athletic 
combat style. He holds a grudge 
against Flashing Steel (1) for 
popularizing "dainty" fighting 
techniques and "stealing his 
students." He and his pupils plan 
to raid their school. Students 
have ADV on Martial Training 
downtime checks with armor 
and versatile/2-handed weapons.

33. BYWATER BARONS
An upstart gang of dock workers 
called the Bywater Barons 
(pg. 44) operates out of a 
ramshackle warehouse at the 
water's edge. Its 50 thugs, led 
by half-orc Yargash the Tall, are 
angry and brazen. They aim to 
dethrone the Thieves' Guild (9), 
which has always had its hands 
in their working-class pockets. 
The Barons have been stealing 
business from the Thieves' Guild 
by offering cheaper protection to 
merchants who use their docks, 
and robbing those who don't.
34. NORLEY'S WARES 
Norley Targon is an indifferent 
merchant who hides a shrewd 
business acumen. His creaky 
old general store is neither too 
showy nor too meager, coming 
off as perfectly ordinary; Norley 
is the city's best illegal goods 
fence because of this. Asking for 
the "deal of the day" is how to 
break through his disinterested 
facade. Selling stolen goods here 
cancels any City Guard pursuit 
for a criminal theft, but there's a 
cumulative 1:6 chance each time 
that Norley betrays the PC to the 
City Guard for that specific item. 
35. CHARITY HOUSE
A looming, two-story manor 
with a wrought iron gate and 
heavy front door. The Charity 
House is a poorly funded branch 
of the Ivory Cathedral (29) 
offering hard beds, thin soup, 
and rudimentary medical care 
to the needy. Matron Bethel, 
a middle-aged woman who is 
nice but not kind, has convinced 
the church's inspector for years 
that all is well. Meanwhile, she's 
been skimming gold off the 
top, and she laces the soup with 
mild poison to keep the patients 
coming. Young Sister Natalie, 
innocent and without authority, 
is starting to suspect the matron 
and fears what it could all mean.   
36. THE RED RAT
A dingy tavern painted garish 
red inside. Local legend says 
a crazed, pipe-playing beggar 
haunts the tunnels beneath the 
tavern (accessible through a trap 
door in the cellar). Drunk patrons 
report hearing a faint tune lilting 
up out of an unknown location. 
PCs who have survived a bout of 
the Rat Plague (see rat, SD pg. 
245) roll an extra mishap and 
benefit when carousing here.

39. GOLDEN VAULT
A bank and secure vault owned 
by a composed and elegant elf 
named Iriel Lanowin. Customers 
can store up to 1,000 gp per level 
here at a fee of 1% of the deposit.  
Iriel's 20 guards patrol the gold-
and-marble building at all hours, 
and she also discreetly pays the 
Thieves' Guild (9) a 5% cut for 
their protection. Iriel is a high-
ranking member of The Shroud. 
40. MALLIN'S FORGE
Mallin Barton is a middle-aged 
weapon smith who gives a nice 
discount to regulars. Mallin 
allows agents of The Onyx Eye, 
the Duke's secret service, to 
operate out of his furnace-like 
cellar. They're circling in on the 
banker Iriel Lanowin (39) for 
suspected links to The Shroud.   
41. MOONLIGHT
A humble jeweler specializing 
in affordable baubles, lucky 
amulets, and everyday jewelry. 
Emeline Torberry loves working 
with silver in particular and can 
craft jewelry of up to 100 gp in 
value. A silver item of hers has 
a 1:20 chance of granting the 
wearer immunity to lycanthropy.
42. CORK & PESTLE
Gomrey Gorn is a middle-aged, 
apron-wearing apothecary 
whose eyebrows are always 
singed off by a mishap with his 
latest experimental concoction. 
One of these days, he'll get the 
formula just right for "the Gom-
Bomb," his pet project to make a 
cube of sticky jelly that explodes 
a few seconds after adhering to 
a hard surface. Once a month, 
a PC can buy 20 gp of rare 
reagents for ADV on a downtime 
check to create a potion.
43. ANVIL HALL
Twin dwarf brothers Homlin and 
Ragrin run the best smithy in 
the city supplied with the finest 
ore from distant Stonehall. Their 
weapons cost triple the normal 
price, but they grant a +1 bonus 
to attack due to their perfectly 
balanced grip and exquisite 
craftsmanship. The plate 
mail they craft is in the hefty 
dwarvish style and triple the 
cost; it occupies an additional 
gear slot and grants +1 AC. The 
brothers have refused to cut in 
the Thieves' Guild (9), and now 
Homlin is slated for "a chat" with 
a guild bruiser as a final warning.

The Rooks District
Class: Working.
Category: Market district.

44. THE RUSTY NAIL
A massive, six-wheeled wagon 
permanently parked and turned 
into a small general goods 
store. Owner Babette Sykes 
decides if she likes a customer 
based on how they treat her two 
affectionate cats, Morkin and 
Tinny. All basic gear is available, 
and each week there's a 1:6 
chance Babette has procured 
a rare consumable magic item 
(spell scroll or potion) she'll sell 
to a good customer for 50 gp.
45. TOUGH NUT
By day, Marjorie Wilkins runs 
a snappy operation out of a 
spacious tent selling eclectic 
trinkets from every corner of the 
realm. Elvish teapots have been 
all the rage lately (15 gp each), 
and giving one as a gift at a first 
meeting adds +1 to the reaction 
roll. Marjorie has little patience 
for questions. By night, her 
brother Geramino takes over, 
a languid hookah-smoker who 
regales shoppers with tales of 
distant lands. He has a knack for 
suggesting the right (expensive) 
gift to impress, allowing a 
reaction check reroll or +1 bonus 
(once per intended recipient).

46. MADAME MORDA
Madame Morda is a white-haired 
old elf who has leaned into the 
lucrative act of being a wizened 
fortune-teller. Burning sage 
fills her tent with a blue haze 
that masks the fake nature of 
her crystal and bone decor. She 
charges 15 gp for a tarot reading, 
50 gp to speak with the dead, 
and 100 gp for a "love potion." It's 
all an expert act of trickery. 
47. THE COOKPOT
Youthful vendor Aron Reese 
does brisk business selling pots 
and pans out of his pristine tent. 
Yet nothing seems to leave the 
display tables; in reality, he sells 
dips of addictive bloodroot (20 
gp), a drug that grant ADV on 
spellcasting checks for a day but 
causes 1d6 CON damage that 
lingers for a month (death at 0). 
48. THE DAISY CHAIN
A rollicking tent tavern draped 
with fresh chains of daisies each 
day. The owner, motherly half-
orc Ygraine Tareek, pays beggar 
children a generous 1 sp for each 
chain they make, to their delight. 
Lawful PCs get a +1 bonus to 
carousing event rolls here.
49. THE BEND
A muddy race track surrounded 
by tents is home to the unofficial 
sport of the city: pig racing. 
Several races take place each 
day, with the best pigs moving 
up to eventually contend in 
the annual Divine Swine race. 
Winning grants the owner 500 
gp and +5 renown. The Divine 
Swine is draped in spring flowers 
and paraded around the city on 
Maytide (pg. 46) with great 
fanfare. Ol' Tangerine, a rotund 
sow with an explosive gallop, is 
the current Divine Swine and the 
pork to beat this year. Her owner, 
nobleman Darien di Morla, will 
do anything to ensure victory.  
50. RUMP ROAST
A sizzling vendor stall wafting 
with spiced meats, pungent pots 
of rare tea, and unrecognizable 
animal carcasses hanging on 
hooks. Owner Leland Putsky 
offers a challenge where anyone 
who eats a raw retch snail and 
keeps it down (DC 15 CON) wins 
20 gp and +2 renown (once only). 
Snake kabobs, the specialty, are 
2 gp and grant +1 on the next 
carousing event roll, but also a 
1:6 chance of food poisoning.

What is Hexcrawl Play?
A hexcrawl is a campaign structure built on three mechanical pillars: 
1. A hex grid  that maps the wilderness
2. Exploration turns  that give travel a procedure
3. Keyed locations  that reward going somewhere new
This book is written for the Game Master (GM), the person who 
builds the map, stocks it with content, and runs the game.
What makes it distinct?
The hex grid gives every location a coordinate and every journey 
a measurable distance.
Keyed hexes mean the GM preps content tied to places, not to a storyline
Each day splits into four watches: morning, afternoon, evening, night.
During each travel watch, the group runs the exploration turn:
pick a direction, check navigation, move, roll for encounters, dis-
cover keyed content, and track resources (rations, torches, gear). 
That loop is the core of hexcrawl play.
The result
Players push into unknown territory, manage their supplies, and 
discover what you’ve placed on the map. What they find depends 
entirely on where they go.
Summary:
• Hexcrawl = hex grid + exploration turns + keyed locations
• The exploration turn gives travel a repeatable procedure
• Content is tied to places on the map, not to a plotline

1. The Journey is the Game
The exploration turn is the core procedure that guides the group 
through the landscape. Think of it like the classic combat round, 
but for travel: a repeatable sequence that creates rhythm.
Each day is divided into four watches (morning, afternoon, evening, 
night), and each watch follows a short checklist: direction, naviga-
tion, movement, encounters, keyed content, resources.
This loop is the game.
Every hex costs something: rations consumed, daylight spent, 
encounter risk taken. But every hex offers something too: a discovery, 
a shortcut, a resource, a story. 
The tension between cost and reward is what makes travel matter. 
Do we push into the swamp before nightfall or camp on dry 
ground? Follow the river or cut through the hills?
Terrain reading, weather shifts, route choices, camp placement:
these are hexcrawl’s equivalent of “I search for traps” and “I check 
the door.” I recommend keeping a visible procedure checklist on 
the table (see the reference card in chapter 3) so the exploration 
turn becomes second nature.
Failure mode: Watches that are just “roll dice, I narrate some walking.”
If there’s no decision in a watch, compress it to one sentence and 
move on.
Summary:
• The exploration turn is the core procedure: a repeatable
  sequence run each watch
• Every hex costs rations, daylight, and risk, but also offers discov- 
 eries and rewards. That tension makes choices real
• A visible checklist on the table makes the procedure automatic

The night is for camp, rest, and guard shifts. The night procedure is 
covered in Step F below.
Three watches of travel per day is the standard pace.
• If a hex takes more than one watch to cross, the party is inside  
 the hex between watches.
• They can still be encountered, they just haven’t reached the   
 other side yet. Mark their position: “halfway through the forest hex.”
• With three travel watches per day and easy terrain, a party can  
 cover three hexes (18 miles).
• In hard terrain, they might not clear a single hex. That’s the 
 resource tension: difficult terrain eats watches, which eats 
 rations, which shortens the expedition.
Step D: Encounter Check
• Roll a d6. On a 1, an encounter occurs (on a 1-2 in dangerous territory). 
 Use your terrain encounter table to determine what they meet.
• The mapper updates the party’s map with whatever they’ve   
 seen this watch: terrain, landmarks, signs of danger. Even on a  
 quiet watch, the mapper should note the terrain type in the hex  
 they’re crossing.

rules.snippet: 27 Step E: Keyed Content If the party enters a keyed hex, describe what they find. This is  where your prep pays off. Read your hex key and bring the loca- tion alive. If the hex is unkeyed, describe the terrain and atmosphere. Nothing  specific happens unless the encounter table says otherwise.  “D
rules.full_text:
27
Step E: Keyed Content
If the party enters a keyed hex, describe what they find. This is 
where your prep pays off. Read your hex key and bring the loca-
tion alive.
If the hex is unkeyed, describe the terrain and atmosphere. Nothing 
specific happens unless the encounter table says otherwise. 
“Dense pine forest, the canopy blocks most of the light. You hear a 
stream somewhere to the east.”
That’s enough.
Step F: Resources
The quartermaster tracks consumption. In a classical fantasy game, 
that looks like this:
• Rations: 1 per person per day (deduct at the end of the day, 
 not per watch)
• Torches: Last 1 hour. Useful for caves and night, but not a full watch
• Lantern + oil flask: Lasts a full watch
• Special gear: Note when situational items are used up (rope left  
 behind, potion consumed, etc.)
Adapt these to your system. The specific items change, but the 
principle stays: every watch spent in the wild costs something.
If rations run out, the party must forage (costs a watch), hunt (costs 
a watch and requires a roll), or turn back. Running out of food deep 
in the wilderness is exactly the kind of crisis that makes hexcrawl 
memorable.
Then start the next watch. Return to Step A and repeat. Each watch 
follows the same six steps until the party camps for the night or 
reaches their destination.

rules.full_text:
33
5. Discovery and Exploration
Keyed content is Step E of the exploration turn. Here’s how to 
bring locations alive.
The best moments in a hexcrawl are when players find something 
unusual and interesting. A crumbling tower on a cliff. A cave behind 
a waterfall. A stone circle humming with energy.
Visible discoveries draw players toward them without the GM needing 
to steer. From high ground, I recommend letting players see land-
marks 2-3 hexes away: a column of smoke, a dark tower, a moun-
tain peak. This gives them reasons to change course and rewards 
climbing hills.
Hidden discoveries reward careful exploration. A buried entrance, a 
concealed path, a camouflaged camp. These require players to say 
“I search the area,” and that engagement is where hexcrawl shines.
When players reach a keyed location, bring it alive:
GM: “You crest the ridge and see it: a stone tower, three stories tall, 
the top floor collapsed. Crows circle the ruin. Fresh scratches on the 
front door frame.”
Players: “We circle it first. Any other entrances?” 
GM: “Around back, a rusted cellar hatch. And bootprints in the 
mud, heading inside.”
Some locations are a single encounter. Others fill a whole session.
Failure mode: Every discovery is a combat encounter. If finding 
things always means fighting, players stop wanting to find things. 
Mix in wonders, resources, clues, and safe discoveries.
Summary:
• High ground should let players see landmarks 2-3 hexes away
• Mix visible and hidden discoveries. Both pull players forward
• Not all discoveries should be dangerous. Wonders and clues   
 matter too

It’s real choices about how to  spend limited resources. Set prices so that a single expedition is af- fordable but a long one hurts.  A rough
rules.full_text:
38
2. Resources and Gold
In a hexcrawl, gold funds the next expedition. That gives it pur-
pose beyond treasure hoarding.
The goal isn’t detailed accounting. It’s real choices about how to 
spend limited resources. Set prices so that a single expedition is af-
fordable but a long one hurts. 
A rough scale: rations cost 1gp per person per day, a porter runs 
5gp per day, a guide who knows the eastern trails costs 20gp, and a 
boat to cross the lake costs 50gp.
• Rations, porters, healing, information, and base improvements  
 should all compete for the same pool of gold.
• 40gp of copper ore from the ravine funds three days of exploration  
 or one porter for a week. That’s a real choice, not bookkeeping.
• I recommend tying gold directly to the map. Every purchase 
 should open new territory or make existing routes safer. 
• A boat lets you cross the lake instead of hiking around it, saving  
 two days.
• Cold-weather gear opens the mountain pass, and what’s up   
 there is worth the cost: rarer finds, stranger ruins, factions no one 
 else has reached.
• A hired scout knows the eastern trails.
Rations and torches are the baseline cost of movement. Gold buys 
the upgrades that change which hexes are reachable. Gold makes 
the map bigger.
Summary:
• Use a rough pricing framework: real choices, not detailed   
 accounting
• Every treasure hoard should connect to the next expedition’s   
 possibilities
• Gold buys capability (boats, porters, info), not power (magic items)

rules.full_text:

7. Long-Term Campaign Tips
Hexcrawl campaigns hit specific walls. Here’s how to handle them:
When the near hexes are all explored: Re-key them. The aban-
doned camp is now occupied, the bridge has been repaired, the lair 
has new inhabitants. Factions move into cleared territory. If players 
have to travel 4+ hexes to find anything new, the early game’s 
density has disappeared.
When players stop caring about resources: Introduce terrain that 
demands specialized gear (boats for coastal hexes, cold-weather 
kits for mountains), but make what’s out there worth the cost: 
richer finds, stranger ruins, factions that can’t be reached any other 
way. If gold piles up with nothing to spend it on, the resource game 
goes slack.
When the rumor board goes stale: Faction movement generates 
new rumors automatically. Returning NPCs (merchants, refugees, 
rival adventurers) bring fresh information from off-map.
When players want to build: Let them establish forward camps, 
claim hexes, and name landmarks. A second base changes the hex 
map’s geometry, creating new frontiers.
When the starting region is fully explored: Expand the map, but 
make expansion earned. Require expensive or rare gear for exotic 
barriers, discovered entrances for underground networks. Treat the 
new region like you did at the start: a handful of major locations, 
seed rumors, let them explore.
You can expand your map for a long time with the techniques in 
this book. When you’re ready to build richer, more interconnected 
regions, The Worldbuilding Guidebook is your next step.

Maybe they’re desperate, or maybe they recognize the party’s gear. The reaction roll forces you out of your prep and into improvisation,  and
rules.full_text:
53
Use the reaction roll to surprise yourself: You keyed this camp as 
“hostile bandits.”
You roll reaction: 9, friendly. Now they’re friendly bandits. Why? 
Maybe they’re desperate, or maybe they recognize the party’s gear.
The reaction roll forces you out of your prep and into improvisation, 
and that’s where the best hexcrawl moments live. The scenes I 
remember most vividly are the ones where the dice contradicted 
my prep and I had to figure out why on the spot.
Connect the encounter to the map:
The lizardfolk traders know a safe route through the swamp. The 
hermit has a crude map of the ravine. The ogre’s lair contains a jour-
nal from a previous expedition. 
Every encounter in a place should point somewhere else on the hex 
map. That’s how exploration builds momentum. Each discovery 
seeds the next expedition.
Failure mode: Locations that are puzzles with one solution, or crea-
tures that exist only to be fought. If players can’t interact with a dis-
covery except through combat, you’ve designed a dungeon room, 
not a hex.
Summary:
• Lead with sensory details and visible motivations, not threats
• Offer multiple approaches: talk, trade, observe. Combat is one 
 option, not the default
• Connect every encounter to the hex map so discoveries build 
 momentum

H
ail, adventurer! 
Welcome to the 
Western Reaches.
You've found yourself in a 
land of fragile civilizations, 
majestic landscapes, and 
secrets lost to the dark.
This realm of mystery and 
wonder is yours. It is a 
place for bold explorers 
who dare to lift a torch 
high in the face of an 
overwhelming night!
The Western Reaches will 
be shaped by your hands.
Warriors and witches, 
mystics and mages. You 
who are true seekers. 
You who follow a hawk 
across the burning desert, 
who chase a river from 
its humble wellspring to 
its mighty crash into the 
sea, and who watch the 
dawn break from atop the 
mountains.
You will discover who you 
are as you explore this 
realm. Will you become 
the land's protector, its 
conquerer? Will its people 
sing ballads or dirges of 
your deeds?
There's only one way to 
find out, of course.
There are many unknown 
paths that lie before you, 
and there is but one thing 
to do: Find your way.
Within these pages, you'll 
meet your beginnings. 
What you will become is 
being written even now as 
you read these words and 
grasp your destiny.
So light your torch, though 
it is a small flame in the 
dark, and let it be known:
You are here, o fabled land!
-Kelsey Dionne, Feb. 2025

rules.full_text:
90
OVERVIEW
Factions are organizations the 
PCs can join that have specific 
missions and bylaws.
PCs who join a faction have the 
opportunity to accrue special 
benefits as long as they remain 
in good standing.
Parties who have multiple PCs 
from the same faction will 
accrue benefits more quickly.
LEADERSHIP
Each faction has an NPC leader 
who holds final authority over 
the faction's members, bylaws, 
and proceedings. 
The faction leader can decide 
the outcome of any disputes 
between members or leave the 
decision up to a majority vote.
A new leader must make a DC 
15 CHA check for a peaceful 
transfer of power. On a failure, 
the faction splinters into 2 
conflicting organizations. 
BEING IN A FACTION
Joining. PCs can join a faction 
by participating in an initiation 
ceremony. A PC can only be in 
one faction at a time and must 
renounce prior factions in order 
to change to a new one.
Standing. PCs remain in good 
standing with a faction as long 
as they follow its bylaws. PCs 
caught breaking the bylaws can 
be expelled from the faction by 
a majority vote of its members or 
by the faction's leader.
PCs who leave a faction lose 
access to its benefits.
Benefits. Combine the levels of 
all PCs in the party who are in 
the same faction to determine 
which faction benefits they gain. 
Only members of the faction 
gain its benefits. 
If a PC leaves the party due to 
any reason other than death, 
subtract their LV from their 
faction's total. This may cause 
the party to lose benefits.
Factions

City of Masks
Members of The Scarlet Bones gather in the 
various seedy bars in the Gutterwash district, but 
so do rival pirate crews looking for trouble.
Alkesh
Pirates are treated as bandits. Shar Yasmila grants 
no mercy to those who disrupt commerce in her 
lands, and so pirates would do well to stay hidden.
Stonehall
Dwarves revile thieves only slightly more than 
they loathe the sea itself. Pirates are seen as crazy 
at best and as irredeemable criminals at worst. 
Kyzian Tribes The Kyzian Princes accept the tradition of plunder 
by force. Pirates have their cautious respect.
Lydonia Piracy is viewed as a crime and distasteful way of 
life. Suspected pirates are arrested and put to trial.

City-State Details
City of Masks
Members meet at The Bull's Pen tavern in 
Silvertop district. They organize forays to pursue 
rumors of treasure and glory in the nearby 
Lowland Moor and The Gloaming.
Alkesh
Torchbearers gather at The Jewel of Borak tavern 
in the Forgotten Quarter. They often plan delves 
into the ancient tunnels beneath the city.
Stonehall
Members are welcome at The Braided Beard 
tavern in The Clanks district where dwarf 
prospectors contract them to clear out dangerous 
mines and investigate weird findings.
Kyzian Tribes
The Kyzian Princes are willing to leave the 
Torchbearers to their adventuring as long as they 
pay a 5% tribute tax to Taru the Hawk Queen on 
any treasure they find in Kyzian lands.
Lydonia
Members host jovial meetings at The Court of 
Mab tavern in the Cerulean Quarter. They are 
viewed as blunt instruments by the noble elves.

rules.full_text:
114
Mounts
RARITY
Mounts are common (C), 
uncommon (U), rare (R), or 
legendary (L). All rarities except 
common  require training to ride.
Rare mounts are difficult to find 
and train. Legendary mounts 
are only found in the wild and 
must be trained from youth.
GEAR SLOTS
Mounts have a number of gear 
slots equal to 5x their STR bonus.
A rider and the rider's carried 
gear (such as a backpack and 
worn items) occupy 10 slots.
MOVEMENT
When riding a mount during 
combat or crawling rounds, use 
its speed for your movement.
Flying. Flying mounts are 
unaffected by difficult or 
impassable terrain, but they 
cannot end overland travel 
movement in impassable terrain. 
PERSONALITY
Most mounts need to make a 
morale check (use rider's CHA) 
when under duress or startled. 
COMBAT
A rider and mount act on the 
rider's initiative. Either the rider 
or mount can take an action on 
the rider's turn (rider decides).
Getting on or off a mount uses 
up your entire movement.
LEVELING UP
A mount gains 1d8 HP per level 
and +1 to attacks on even levels.
FEEDING MOUNTS
Mounts find their own rations in 
familiar environments if they are 
allowed to graze. For instance, 
camels can subsist in the desert.
Mounts must be given a ration 
each day in an environment they 
are not accustomed to enduring, 
such as camels in the arctic.

Tier 3, wizard (C)

FREYA BOONS
The neutral Old God of love and 
hatred. The Queen of Shield 
Maidens whose valkyries carry 
worthy souls who died in battle 
to the Great Feast in Valhalla. 
The First Seer who places her 
omens in bones, blood, and 
entrails. Freya inspires the poets 
with creative passion and then 
torments them with its lack.

nords give deference to Freya

rules.full_text:

Hex Crawling
TRAVEL PER DAY
Hexes are 6-miles across. The 
PCs can enter a number of hexes 
per day based on travel method.
MOVEMENT
PCs move from hex to hex as a 
group while traveling overland. 
Shift into combat or crawling 
rounds if an encounter occurs. 
Check for a random encounter 
twice a day and twice overnight 
with a 1:6 chance each time. Roll 
a d12 to determine what time of 
day the encounters happen. 
WEATHER
Check the weather each day by 
rolling a d6. 
On a 1, the weather is stormy. 
Normal terrain becomes difficult 
for one day. In a harsh climate, 
(see pg. 42), terrain becomes 
impassable for one day instead. 
On a 6, the weather is excellent. 
Roll the next weather with ADV.
FOOD AND WATER
PCs and mounts must each 
consume one ration per day, 
taking 1 CON damage (death at 
0) if they do not. A PC can forage 
for 1 ration a day during travel 
with an INT check.
PUSHING
At the start of the day, the PCs 
can choose to push to multiply 
their hexes per day by 1.5 times. 
Increase the random encounter 
chance by 1:6 that day. PCs can't 
forage on a day they push.
Travel Method Hexes per Day
Walking 4
Mounted 6
Sailing 8*
ENTERING HEXES
Terrain Hex Cost to Enter
Normal 1
Difficult 2
Impassable Cannot enter
TERRAIN TYPES
*See pg. 118 for variable boat speeds

rules.full_text:
228
Climate
The Western Reaches are home 
to a wide variety of climates 
and that can pose dangers to 
adventurers.
Most regions have moderate 
weather in the spring and fall. 
The weather is the most severe 
in the summer  and winter. 
HARSH CLIMATE
Some seasons and regions bring 
challenging survival conditions.
On the Climate In The Reaches 
Table, entries with a dagger† 
have a harsh climate at all times. 
Entries with an asterisk* have 
a harsh climate only during 
stormy weather (see pg. 226). 
In a harsh climate:
• Each PC and mount must 
consume double rations or be 
treated as if they consumed 
none today.
• Trying to forage or hunt is 
DC 18 in normal weather and 
impossible in stormy weather.
ISLES OF ANDRIK
This northernmost part of the 
Western Reaches experiences 
full seasons of long-term day 
and night.
Midnight Sun. Spring and 
summer. The sun never fully 
sets. There is enough light to see 
clearly outside at all hours.
Harvest. Fall. Sunny during the 
day and dark at night.
Long Dark. Winter. Night 
never ends. Only dark-adapted 
creatures can see without light.
UNDERGROUND
In the depths of the earth, there 
are neither seasons nor weather. 
Instead, these deep tunnels 
are humid and cool year round, 
never changing in a way that 
drives creatures of the sun mad. 
When the season changes on 
the surface, PCs far underground 
must pass DC 12 CHA checks or 
take 1d4 CHA damage.

230
Camping
Optionally, characters can 
choose to undertake camping 
procedures during a rest.
CAMPFIRE
The PCs can make a campfire 
using 3 torches; it lasts 8 hours 
while a PC remains near to it and 
casts light out to a near distance. 
Without a campfire, the PCs 
have DISADV on tasks marked 
with an asterisk*.  
TASKS
Each PC can do one task while 
camping and still get a full rest. 
PCs can do the same task.
The GM determines the DC of 
each task check based on the 
situation. Default to DC 12.
Bed Down.* WIS or CON. You 
do not need to make checks to 
benefit from rest if your sleep is 
interrupted during this rest.
Cook.* INT or WIS. Each PC who 
consumes a ration gains +2 
temporary HP that lasts 1 day.
Craft.* DEX. Create 2d4 pieces of 
mundane weapon ammunition 
or one torch. Alternatively, repair 
a broken piece of mundane gear.
Entertain*. CHA. Grant 1 luck 
token to another PC.
Firewood. STR or CON. Make one 
free campfire this rest without 
expending torches. 
Hunt. STR or DEX. Find 1d4 
rations. You cannot hunt if you 
pushed during today's travel. 
Keep Watch.* WIS. You cannot 
be surprised during one half of 
the rest (you choose which). 
Predict. INT or WIS. You may 
force a re-roll of tomorrow's 
weather after learning the result. 
PROCEDURE
1. The PCs make task checks in 
any order they choose.
2. After resolving tasks, the 
GM follows normal resting and 
random encounter procedures.

rules.full_text:
231
Fast Travel
OVERVIEW
The GM may allow the PCs to 
fast travel between two hexes 
they have previously entered. 
The PCs must travel between 
these points through hexes they 
have already explored; they can't 
pass through unexplored hexes.
TIME
The GM estimates the time 
needed for the PCs to reach their 
destination per the table below. 
The GM should factor in the 
travel method (mounted, sailing, 
etc.), distance, and terrain.
When needing a specific time 
length, roll 2d6 per estimated 
week of travel to determine how 
many days the journey takes.
RATIONS
The PCs must eat the minimum 
number of rations required if 
they have them available. 
PCs who cannot eat the required 
number of rations arrive drained.
Drained. You take CON damage 
equal to half your current CON 
score (round down). You have 
DISADV on all checks and attack 
rolls until you successfully rest. 
One PC can make an INT check 
(GM sets the DC based on region 
and climate) to scavenge during 
the journey. On a success, the 
group avoids arriving drained.
PROCEDURE
1. The GM estimates the time 
needed for the journey. 
2. One PC may make an INT 
check to scavenge for the group.
3. The PCs reach their intended 
destination. They arrive drained, 
if applicable.
Time Needed Min. Rations
A few days 1-3
About a week 3
Several weeks 3/week
FAST TRAVEL

Travel Procedure
Step 1: Weather. Roll a d6 to 
determine the weather.
Step 2: Visible Hexes. Determine 
which hexes the PCs can see.
Step 3: Travel Method. The PCs 
decide their mode of travel.
Step 4: Travel Speed. The PCs 
decide whether to move at 
normal speed or push.
Step 5: Traveling. The PCs move, 
expending as much available 
movement as they want. Update 
the visible hexes as they travel. 
Step 6: Traveling Encounters. 
Check for and trigger random 
encounters while the PCs travel.
Step 7: Resting. Optionally, the 
PCs may camp . They can forage 
for rations if they didn't push. 
They consume rations (double if 
in a harsh climate) and rest.
Step 8: Resting Encounters. 
Check for and trigger random 
encounters while the PCs rest.

Downtime
PCs can do one downtime 
activity between adventures. 
Activities marked with an 
asterisk* cost 50 gp per attempt.  
To succeed on a downtime 
activity, a character must pass 
the associated check. PCs can't 
use luck tokens on these checks.
If a PC fails a check, reduce its 
DC one step the next time they 
attempt it (reset after success).
SPIRITUALISM
Meditation, prayer, self-
reflection, or mystical study.
WIS Check
• DC 9: Gain favor with a 
local church. Your renown 
increases by 1 point.
• DC 12: Spiritual strengthening. 
You gain 2 XP.
• DC 15*: Find personal insight. 
Reroll one prior talent roll. 
• DC 18*: Spiritual cleansing. 
End one curse afflicting you.
SKULDUGGERY
Thievery, criminal activity, or 
churning the rumor mill. 
CHA Check
• DC 9: Start a rumor about 
one person. Their renown 
increases or decreases by 1 
point (you choose).
• DC 12: Lay low. Escape the 
authorities over a small crime.
• DC 15: Extortion. Increase the 
value of your next sale by 25%, 
or reduce the cost of your 
next purchase by 25%. 
• DC 18: Hide out. Escape the 
authorities over a big crime.
DEX Check
• DC 15: Get away with a minor 
crime, such as petty theft. If 
you fail, the crime fails and 
the authorities investigate.
• DC 18*: Get away with a major 
crime, such as murder. If you 
fail, the crime fails and the 
authorities investigate.

constructed by paying its cost.

and HP. At 0 HP, the bastion's

MASS COMBAT
A warband is a group of up to 20 
similar combatants. Treat it as a 
single creature. A warband that 
falls to 0 HP is destroyed.  
Attacks. A warband's attacks 
fill a near-sized area around 
its target. It can disperse its 
damage dice between anything 
it would hit within that area. 
Unique Beings. PCs and level 6+ 
creatures act as individuals. A 
warband can't target or disperse 
damage dice to unique beings 
that are also in a warband (other 
unique beings can still do so).
Initiative. Warbands act on their 
commander's turn in any order. 
Morale. A warband uses its 
commander's CHA bonus for 
morale checks. It checks morale 
when it falls to half HP and each 
time it takes damage while 
below half HP. On a failure, it 
has a 3:6 chance of a rout (being 
destroyed while fleeing). 
Leadership. If you join one of 
your warbands, it has ADV on 
morale checks. You move with it 
but act independently. 
MAINTAINING
Cost. A warband costs 10 gp x 
its level each month to feed and 
maintain. If you are in arrears, 
the warband makes a morale 
check each week. Upon a failure, 
the warband deserts.
Healing. Warbands heal 1d4 HP 
per day unless otherwise noted.
Retraining. You can change the 
upgrades your warbands have. 
Doing so takes 1 week.
RECRUITING
As a downtime activity, you can 
try to recruit a warband equal 
to your level or less (also see 
Recruiting Limits below).
Choose a warband and make 
a CHA check equal to 10 + the 
warband's level. On a success, 
you recruit the new warband.

rules.full_text:
7
WHAT IS 
SHADOWDARK?
Shadowdark RPG is a fantasy 
adventure game where you 
and your companions delve 
into buried ruins, lost cities, 
spider-infested forests, and even 
fearsome dragon lairs in search 
of gold and glory. 
The Shadowdark is any place 
where danger and darkness hold 
sway. It clutches ancient secrets 
and dusty treasures in its rotting 
claws, daring fortune seekers to 
tempt their fates.
With your adventuring 
companions at your side, you 
confront the Shadowdark's 
sinister traps, formidable magics, 
and ruthless monsters.
If you survive, you'll bring back 
untold riches plucked from 
the jaws of death itself. And 
before long, you'll hear the 
Shadowdark's call once again! 
WHAT DEFINES THIS 
GAME?
Speed, danger, and simplicity. 
Magic is perilous, and battles are 
fast and deadly. Being clever is 
crucial for survival.
Shadowdark RPG is rules-light 
and intuitive. It encourages 
quick decisions rather than 
hunting through the rulebook 
for answers.
In this game, a torch only holds 
back the pressing darkness for 
one hour of real-world time. 
There isn’t a moment to waste 
when the flames are burning 
low...
HOW DO I PLAY?
Everything you need to play 
or run a game is in this tome. 
Turn to the next section to get 
familiar with the basics!
Shadowdark

rules.full_text:
8
If this is your first time playing 
Shadowdark RPG, it’s helpful to 
start with a premade character. 
The free digital Shadowdark 
RPG Quickstart Set has a few!
CHARACTERS
You decide your character’s 
actions and tell them to the 
referee, or Game Master (GM). 
The GM determines if your 
actions are successful and 
describes the results.
This back-and-forth between 
you, the GM, and your 
adventuring companions grows 
and shapes the game world.
Always ask yourself: If you were 
really your character, what 
would you do right now?
DESCRIBE AN 
ACTION
On your turn, describe an action 
you want to do. For example, you 
could say you’re going to shoot 
your bow at a troll.
The GM might ask you to do a 
check (see Checks) to determine 
whether your action succeeds.
MOVEMENT
During your turn, you can move 
up to near (roughly 30 feet). You 
can break this movement up 
in any way. If you don’t take an 
action, you can move near again.
ROUNDS
Each person takes a turn, 
starting with the GM and going 
clockwise. The GM controls the 
monsters and environment and 
narrates how everyone’s actions 
change the game world.
Once everyone has taken a turn, 
that completes one round. Then, 
a new round begins.
The Basics

rules.snippet: 44 Casting Spells Spellcasters use the raw power  of creation and destruction to  bend reality, shaping it to the  will of their gods or ambitions. Wizard magic is fickle,  complicated, and volatile. Even  the most learned mages tread  carefully when reaching beyond  the veil to grasp arcane energie
rules.full_text:
44
Casting Spells
Spellcasters use the raw power 
of creation and destruction to 
bend reality, shaping it to the 
will of their gods or ambitions.
Wizard magic is fickle, 
complicated, and volatile. Even 
the most learned mages tread 
carefully when reaching beyond 
the veil to grasp arcane energies.
Priest magic is miraculous, 
sacred, and instinctive. Priests 
who offend their gods might 
lose the ability to cast spells until 
they can undertake penance. 
SPELLCASTING
When you cast a spell, you 
invoke magic to cause an effect. 
Casting a spell takes your action.
Characters with the spellcasting 
talent can cast spells. 
To cast a wizard spell you know, 
make a spellcasting check by 
rolling 1d20 + your Intelligence 
modifier. 
To cast a priest spell you know, 
make a spellcasting check by 
rolling 1d20 + your Wisdom 
modifier.
The DC to successfully cast a 
spell is 10 + the spell’s tier.
RESULTS
If you succeed on your 
spellcasting check, the spell 
takes effect.
If you fail your spellcasting 
check, the spell does not take 
effect. You can’t cast that spell 
again until you complete a rest.

check.
CRITICAL FAILURE

Wizard Spell. If the spell was a 
wizard spell, you can’t cast that 
spell again until you successfully 
complete a rest. You must also 
roll on the Wizard Mishap table 
corresponding to the spell’s tier 
(see pg. 46).

a priest spell, your deity is 
greatly displeased and revokes 
its power. You can’t cast that 
spell again until you complete 
ritualistic penance to your deity 
and successfully complete a rest.
PENANCE
The GM determines the exact 
nature of the penance you must 
undertake based on your deity 
and alignment. 
Penance requires a holy 
quest, ritualistic atonement, 
or a material sacrifice that you 
donate or destroy. 
Inadequate or subversive 
penance (such as donating your 
sacrifice to a party member) only 
displeases your deity further and 
makes the spell loss permanent.

rules.full_text:
