fluff.full_text:
30
1010. OFFERING STATUES
Six leering, bat-faced statues 
(gargoyles) perch at the point 
where the tunnel splits into 
two major arteries. Clay bowls 
of dried blood, bound skeletal 
remains, and four rubies (200 gp 
each) lie at their feet. An offering 
of living flesh or 200 gp sates the 
gargoyles, allowing safe passage.   
1105. GRIZZENGHAST
A lightless city rises above the 
Abyss (1005), clinging to its 
precipice like a roosting harpy. 
Its stone towers snake drunkenly 
upward, twisted and precarious, 
lashed together by cords of 
morzo moth silk. Here, 3,000 
gray-skinned fiends called the 
dremir make their home. The 
streets are wet and serpentine, 
and a grim quiet prevails, for the 
eyeless dremir are sensitive to 
noise and flame. They silently 
crowd visitors, grinning painfully, 
but always keeping at arm's 
length as required by their laws. 
They are a people wealthy in 
sorcerous knowledge, crafting, 
and culture. A visitor is safe for 
three days total in a month; 
the moment this expires, the 
ravenous dremir fall upon them.    
1109. NIGHTBOUND SEA
Churning waves break against 
the black pebble beach of this 
underground sea. The reek 
of algae and decay boils off 
its surface. Monolithic basalt 
pillars thrust from the foul 
water like towers, each carved 
with spiraling glyphs. Deep 
below the surface, one of The 
Lost gods rests on the seafloor, 
bound in ever-burning chains 
forged by Madeera and Memnon 
together in their only act of 
unity. Wretched aboleths and 
aquatic brain eaters attend to 
this titanic god as it lies in silent 
repose, neither dead nor alive.
1202. RALK'S CHIMNEY
A faint, gray glow at the top 
of this vast cavern hints at an 
exit to the sunlit surface. This 
miles-long, narrowing chimney 
is named after the legendary 
thief Ralk, the only person to 
ever survive its treacherous 
climb. Scaling the chimney takes 
four days and requires pinning 
oneself to the wall to sleep, 
often alongside the rope-bound 
corpses of other failed climbers. 
Giant spiders and morzo moths 
nest all along its perilous walls.

fluff.full_text:
38
ROOM KEY
The keyworded descriptions at the start of each location are safe to 
share with the players. The bulleted details beneath are for the GM. 
Overview
BACKGROUND
Nobody knows where the grinning Librarians of Leng came from. 
These creatures might be demons, or they might even be living 
manifestations of the Shadowdark's madness. They have dwelt in 
the Library since time long forgotten, deep in the darkness, never to 
be seen by mankind. There, they catalogue the nightmares, terrors, 
and fears that flow through this dimension. The Librarians of Leng 
know a crucial fact about every being who has walked this world: 
what they fear most. To some, there is no greater treasure.  
FACTIONS
Librarians of Leng. Masters of the Library. Keepers of the deep lore. 
These blindfolded beings stalk in silk robes through ancient halls. 
Captive deep ones, trolls, and gargoyles serve them. Horrid grins 
twist their faces; they can make no other expression than painful joy.
Prisoners. Trespassers, deep delvers, and wizards who teleported to 
the wrong place. The Librarians lock up any intruders so their fears 
can be provoked and studied. Prisoners who still cling to sanity are 
united in their desire to escape, setting all else aside.
Books. Some sentient books do not want to be housed in the 
Library of Leng, so they seek a way out. Many are self-serving and 
will only keep alliances for as long as they are convenient. Others are 
noble and wish their knowledge to be returned to the world.

fluff.full_text:
40
Rumors
1
The King of the Ivory Palace's daughter opened a forbidden 
book that transported her to the Library of Leng. He seeks a 
swift rescue before word gets out that Yarina is missing.
2
The demonic warlord Gazalaaru's only weakness is the secret 
phobia he suffers, knowledge he protects with potent magic. 
Only the Library of Leng could reveal this invaluable secret.
3
The famed bard Sakar the Enlightened can no longer 
perform due to stage fright from an intractable curse a fey 
queen laid upon him. Magical help has utterly failed. Is there 
another way to aid him within the Library of Leng?
4
The mighty Tome of Gehemna has fallen into the hands of 
the Librarians of Leng! It is too precious to the mages of this 
world to stay locked in the Library; it must be liberated. 
5
The wizards of Gedgarrin are forging a mighty arrow to snuff 
the life of the sea dragon Trastaviing, who has terrorized the 
coast for far too long. The final spell requires uttering the 
dragon's greatest fear, but even the gods will not disclose this 
knowledge to the wizards in portents or divinations.
6
The Librarians of Leng are said to possess a primordial beast 
called a bezelak that they nurture and worship. This particular 
specimen must be ancient and housing several bezoar stones 
in its stomach, which are more valuable than diamonds! 
7
Even the mightiest beings hold a measure of respect for the 
Librarians of Leng. The Librarians may be willing to serve as 
intermediaries between the PCs and such a being, for a price. 
8
The Mother of Night comes in dreams to demand the rescue 
of Anamaxis, one of her favored daughters, from entrapment 
in the Library of Leng. Obey her and receive a powerful boon.
RUMORS

fluff.full_text:
42
2. GUARD ROOM
A bestial, winged statue hunches over a table scattered with 
tiny white objects and whispers: "355... 356... 356... curses, double 
counted!" A corkscrewing lever juts from the wall behind him.
• Statue. A twitchy gargoyle named Grimgald. He compulsively re-
counts his bag of 492 mouse bones (or is it 493?). He guards the 
portcullis in Area 1 but is distracted (DC 12 DEX to sneak by him). 
 ▶ Grimgald assumes PCs are visitors. He ushers them to Area 4 to 
wait while he fetches his master Achocklak (Area 24). Grimgald 
and Achocklak return to Area 4 in 5 rounds.
 ▶ Key. Grimgald wears the brass key to Area 28 on a neck cord.
• Lever. A spiraling tentacle shape. Operates the portcullis in Area 1. 
3. GARGOYLE ROOST
Five statues of leering, winged demons lean out from high perches. 
Piles of moss grow on their heads and shoulders like snow.
• Demons.  Off-duty gargoyle guards who have enjoyed 50 years of 
rest after Grimgald (Area 2) lost a bet to them. They roost on 20' 
cave shelves. Loud noise wakes them (disoriented 1d4 rounds).
 ▶ Gargoyles: Icarus (bully), Regaran (drowsy), Hestia (gluttonous), 
Molossus (academic), Trivonus (vain). 
4. WAITING ROOM
Red velvet reading chairs gather dust beside crowded book shelves. 
A few glittering trinkets sit on a low parlor table. 
• Books. Grim fables about never trusting anyone ("The Hidden 
Knife," "Betrayal of Brothers"). "The Watcher" is a sentient book 
and tattle-tale; it spies on visitors and reports what they said to 
Achocklak (Area 24). It shrilly interrogates people if opened.
• Trinkets. Dry ink pots, paper weights, crystals. Among these is a 
silver spinning top (1/day, spin for 1:4 chance to gain a luck token).

8. SKULL CAVE
Countless gaping skulls line the walls of this vast cathedral cave. At 
its center, a monumental pillar of stone climbs from floor to ceiling. 
• Skulls. Thousands of humanoids. Each has a clay tablet inside its 
eye socket engraved with that person's worst fear (spiders, the 
sea, Auntie Nellie, leeches, the Willowman, public speaking, etc.).
 ▶ Two skulls have 500 gp diamonds instead (30 minutes to find 
each). Images of cavorting demons dance inside the gems.
• Pillar. A secret door opens to a slippery, corkscrewing tunnel (DC 
18 DEX to stop/climb) that chutes creatures 60' down into Area 50.
• Ritual. The first time the PCs enter this area, throaty chanting 
(many voices) rises from the eastern passage.
 ▶ 4 Librarians of Leng and 8 deep ones drag 4 pale, ragged 
peasants (lost explorers) in chains to this room from Area 14. 
The peasants are drugged with Vapor of Leng (see Area 20).
 ▶ The Librarians release the peasants in Area 8 and observe for 5 
rounds as they attack each other in drug-addled terror. Then, 
the deep ones shove them through the secret door in the pillar.
9. ARGUING DEEP ONES
Angry gibbering, wet slaps, and caterwauling echoes from this cave. 
A group of bulge-eyed, fish-faced men stand in a circle furiously 
pointing their webbed claws at each other.
• Men. 6 deep ones argue savagely in the Merran tongue about 
whose fault it is they forgot to bring the key to the door. They 
are distracted and do not notice anything except loud sounds or 
direct intrusions.
 ▶ One carries a note written in elegant hand: "Make sure that 
damned stingbat infestation has been eradicated. -Xenoxes"
 ▶ After 3 rounds, the deep ones leave in a huff to retrieve the key 
from Area 49. They return with it in 10 rounds.

("Principles of Alchemical Bonds,"  "Ethereal-Dimensional Threads," "Transmogrifying Elements,"  "Harnessing Psychic Emanations"). An INT-bas
fluff.full_text:

23. STUDY
A large alcove houses a collection of books. Slightly too-tall desks 
and leather reading chairs line the walls.
• Books. Arcane texts, very dry. ("Principles of Alchemical Bonds," 
"Ethereal-Dimensional Threads," "Transmogrifying Elements," 
"Harnessing Psychic Emanations"). An INT-based spellcaster who 
studies at least 3 of these books during their downtime gains +1 
to spellcasting checks (once only). 
24. SENSORY DEPRIVATION CHAMBER
A black void of utter silence lies beyond the threshold of the door. A 
thin, red string emerges from the darkness along the ground.  
• Void. Magical silence and darkness blanket the room. Even dark-
adapted creatures can't see inside it. Achocklak, a Librarian of 
Leng, meditates within.
 ▶ Achocklak. Shrewd, suspicious. Speaks slowly and deliberately. 
Believes all the gargoyles (Areas 2 and 3) are idiots and resents 
being their keeper. He has a master key to all locked areas. 
• String. Tied around Achocklak's finger. Pulling it summons him 
from his meditations. 
25. STATUE OF LENG
A life-sized, black marble statue of a man stands on a plinth. Dozens 
of small tokens are scattered around its base.
• Statue. A human wizard with a tired smile. He displays his palm, 
which has an eye in it. He holds a real book under his other arm. 
A plaque in Primordial says: "Archmage Leng, Oracle of the Lost."
 ▶ Book. The Tome of Gehemna (SD pg. 318). Taking it causes 
the tome to awaken from a torpor. It pleads to be returned to 
Mordanticus in the Library of Gehemna where it belongs.
• Tokens. Various eyes made of glass, metal, amber, and bone. 
Leaving an eye-shaped offering grants a luck token (1/week).

Each closely details the life of every dragon that has ever  lived. It takes 4 rounds to find a specific dragon by name.  ▶ Reading

33. BOOKS OF DRAGONS
Black mahogany bookshelves reach to the ceiling. They house a few 
hundred tomes bound in pebbled reptile skin of jewel-toned colors. 
• Tomes.  Each closely details the life of every dragon that has ever 
lived. It takes 4 rounds to find a specific dragon by name.
 ▶ Reading. Books are in Draconic. 3:6 chance that opening one 
unleashes a dragon breath weapon at the opener matching the 
book's coloration. Reading at least 3 tomes grants the reader a 
permanent boon of fireblood, frostblood, or stormblood (once 
per reader, see dragon talents, SD pg. 210-211).
 ▶ Draconification. Stealing a book causes the thief to gradually 
turn into a wyvern over 2d6 days (reverses if book is returned).
• Secret Door. To Area 31.
34. BOOKS OF MORTALS
A dense forest of teetering, stacked books spirals toward the ceiling. 
The books are a wild mess of different colors, shapes, and materials. 
• Books. Each is a log of the fears of every member of a mortal 
family line (all ancestries). Finding a specific book takes 4 hours 
without a Librarian of Leng, who can find any title instantly.
 ▶ Reading. Tomes are in the relevant ancestry's language. Several 
books have purple ink blotting out entries; this ink (from Area 
59) can erase a fear from the book, erasing it in real life as well.
35. CHECKOUT DESK
A 9-foot tall, purple-skinned being in yellow silk robes slumps at a 
stone desk with his hand on his chin, tapping his fingers.
• Being. A young and bored Librarian of Leng named Terkule on 
checkout desk duty. Has a one-sided grudge against Cirroc (Area 
61) over a forgotten insult and wants to see him humiliated.
• Desk. Cluttered with books. Bottle of Magic Ink (SD pg. 306).

fluff.source: Cursed Scroll 5 - Dwellers in the Deep V1-3.pdf
fluff.snippet: 54 36. CURIO MUSEUM Dozens of orderly wall niches each display a unique trinket. • Trinkets. Most are worthless novelties from the surface world.  Plaques describe each object and its "far-flung" origin. Tea cup,  magnifying glass, pinned butterfly, demon mask, horse shoe, etc.     ▶ Blue Cube. 4 in
fluff.full_text:
54
36. CURIO MUSEUM
Dozens of orderly wall niches each display a unique trinket.
• Trinkets. Most are worthless novelties from the surface world. 
Plaques describe each object and its "far-flung" origin. Tea cup, 
magnifying glass, pinned butterfly, demon mask, horse shoe, etc.   
 ▶ Blue Cube. 4 inches wide, metallic. Touching it to a living 
creature allows wielder to transform into that creature for up to 
10 rounds a day. Cube can hold one memorized transformation 
at a time; wielder can change it to a new creature.   
37. REFRESHMENTS CHAMBER
A lone imp wearing a blue velvet tailcoat sits in the middle of a long 
dining table and saws tunelessly on a viol. Trays of dainty appetizers 
and silver ewers full of dark liquids surround him.
• Imp.  Smellik, a burdensome "gift" from a visiting demon prince. 
The Librarians of Leng don't know what to do with him and have 
DISADV on spellcasting while he's playing viol within earshot.
• Appetizers. Crab cakes, aboleth roe, seared cave slug. All slimy. 
• Ewers. Morzo moth milk. DC 12 CON per gulp or drunk 10 rounds.
38. BOOKS OF DEMONS
Black shelves are crammed with tomes bound in crudely stitched 
skins, sheets of metal, or oily leathers. Room reeks of sulfur.
• Tomes.  Written in Diabolic and sorted randomly. Each is a first-
person autobiography from the perspective of a demon; it 
updates even while being read. Finding a specific book takes 2 
hours (a Librarian of Leng can find any title instantly).
 ▶ Mirror-Bound Tome. The Princess of the Ivory Palace, Yarina 
Tesura, is trapped inside a book with a mirrored cover. The 
pages narrate as a demon relentlessly chases her. The only way 
to free her is by writing a new sentence into the book narrating 
her escape with the Purple Ink from Area 59.

On sorting duty as  punishment after trying to tame a stingbat (wants one as a pet). • Carts. Ordinary books mixed with 2 sentient bo
fluff.full_text:

39. SORTING ROOM
A muttering, long-limbed being in green silk robes trudges around 
depositing books onto wheeled carts.
• Being. A Librarian of Leng named Hakiri. On sorting duty as 
punishment after trying to tame a stingbat (wants one as a pet).
• Carts. Ordinary books mixed with 2 sentient books who want to 
escape the Library. They whisper entreaties to potential allies.
 ▶ "Dimensional Tunneling" (nerdy about space-time; contains 
a Spell Scroll of Dimension Door), "Training Trolls" (strict and 
disciplined; all trolls have DISADV to attack the book's wielder).
40. BOOKS OF ANGELS
Marble columns and stained glass panels form bookshelves that 
hold glittering ivory tomes. A note is pinned near the door.
• Tomes.  Alabaster and mother-of-pearl bindings. Illuminated 
manuscripts in Celestial. Each details the holy deeds of an angel. 
Perfect organization allows any book to be found in 5 rounds. 
• Note. "To all scholars: Research indicates angels do not harbor 
inborn fears. Headmaster Xenoxes will purchase a captured angel 
(1,000 gp) to subject to fear-inculcation experiments."
41. BLACK ORB
In this chilly, silent room, a statue of a 15-foot tall Librarian of Leng 
holds out a clawed hand; a black orb hovers over its open palm.
• Trap. Trying to open any door into Area 41 without wearing the 
Talisman of Leng (Area 59) teleports the being to Area 50.
• Orb. A 3-foot wide Sphere of Annihilation (SD pg. 315). Librarians 
of Leng have ADV on INT checks to move it.
• Statue. If anyone tries to move the Sphere, the statue vies for 
control of it (+4 INT bonus and ADV) and targets PCs. It can not 
control the Sphere once the orb moves outside of Area 41.

DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open. • Prison Cell. Holds subjects of the Librarians' torturous research.  ▶ Angel. An unarmored, weaponless archa
fluff.full_text:

54. PRISONERS
Two dark shapes crouch inside a heavily barred prison cell. Quiet 
whimpers and the occasional hysterical shriek erupt from within.
• Locked Doors. DC 20 DEX/18 STR to open.
• Prison Cell. Holds subjects of the Librarians' torturous research.
 ▶ Angel. An unarmored, weaponless archangel named Apolion. 
His wings are shorn and crudely stitched (can move near). 
Experimental fear conditioning has at last broken him; he is 
madly terrified of beetles and believes they are everywhere. 
 ▶ Gorilla. An intelligent gorilla named Tektumi (pragmatic and 
long-suffering, ruefully accepts his fate). He is wary friends with 
Apolion and contemplates putting the angel out of his misery.
• Curtain. Leads to an observation platform 40' high over the cave 
in Area 53. The underside of the platform is greased regularly with 
tallow (pg. 22), making it too slippery to climb.
55. TIME DILATION ZONE
The air trembles with a subtly disorienting motion. Flickering 
shadows stutter and sometimes reverse their movement. 
• Time Instability. Passing through this area causes all timed 
effects (including torches) to randomly reset to a new duration.
• Secret Door. In southeastern hallway. Goes to Area 56.
56. HIDDEN WATCHPOST
A lanky, purple-skinned being in blue robes holds its silk-wrapped 
head against the arrow slits along the walls, listening intently.
• Being. A Librarian of Leng monitors Area 30 through arrow slits 
hidden from the outside.
 ▶ Hostile. Librarian immediately attacks any creatures outlined in 
the green aura from the door trap in Area 29.
• Secret Door. To southeastern hallway of Area 55.

They exit to remote areas:  a lush tropical jungle, a glaringly bright desert, a mist-choked  forest, a pebble beach dusted in snow, and a vast cathedral cave.      ▶ Retur
fluff.full_text:

63. DISTANT PORTALS
Translucent ovals lined in blue light float inside each alcove.
• Ovals. Portals to far-flung locations. They exit to remote areas: 
a lush tropical jungle, a glaringly bright desert, a mist-choked 
forest, a pebble beach dusted in snow, and a vast cathedral cave.    
 ▶ Return. The portals disappear behind users unless a person 
crossing through wears the Talisman of Leng (Area 59).
64. WENDEL STABLES
Two cow-sized slugs with spiny carapaces trawl the room, slurping 
up bloody piles of chopped meat. They wear riding saddles.
• Wendels. Two spiny wendels trained for Librarian of Leng riders. 
DC 15 CHA for others to ride (recheck each time wendel is under 
duress or startled). On a failure, the wendel attacks the rider.
 ▶ Lil' Sweetie. Friendly, food-motivated, hideously cute.
 ▶ Baylight. Scintillating brown hide, skeptical, hates deep ones.

The city where  all stories begin and end!  Let your eye climb up  along the cliffs where  the mighty river meets  the
fluff.full_text:
9
T
he golden light of 
dawn yet washes 
over the towers of 
the grand City of Masks!
There it is before you, in all 
its sun-kissed glory. When 
agone have you seen such 
majesty? The city where 
all stories begin and end! 
Let your eye climb up 
along the cliffs where 
the mighty river meets 
the sea. Up and up, over 
white sails and swooping 
canals, up to the bridges 
and glinting rooftops that 
chain like the pendant 
of jewels laying over the 
heart of Madeera herself.
There, on the highest 
hill, the red banners of 
Montmar Castle  flutter 
proudly in the sea breeze. 
It is within those walls that 
the Duke presides, noble 
and steadfast, his hand 
lifting us all beside him.
Up there, too, in the deep 
shadows of forgotten 
back alleys and streets, 
dark souls burn with their 
own wicked passions. For 
no city of epic deeds can 
claim that all are done for 
the good of mankind. 
Nay, in the City of Masks, 
even great evil lashes with 
silver tongue, cuts with 
skilled blade, and kills with 
unmatched artistry.  
So what will you choose in 
this place of our best and 
worst natures? Will we one 
day sing a ballad of your 
arrival, or a dirge?
Here, your deeds each 
become a new mask you 
wear. A new story, a new 
player on the stage.
Wear your masks true, and 
wear them well!
-Kelsey Dionne, Oct. 2025

even to regular folks. You're not 
welcome in upscale places.
4-7. Gain a +1 renown bonus on 
carousing event rolls. Regular 
folk view you favorably. People 
of high status ignore you, 
especially in upscale places.
8-11. Gain a +2 renown bonus 
on carousing event rolls. You're 
a known name. High-status 
people treat you as a peer.
12+. Gain a +3 renown bonus on 
carousing event rolls. You're a 
celebrity, welcome in the most 
luxurious of places. People of 
high status defer to you.
GAINING RENOWN
PCs gain a point of renown each 
time the following occurs:
• Gaining a level
• Being honored publicly
• Extravagant public spending
• A major triumph or success
LOSING RENOWN
PCs lose a point of renown each 
time the following occurs:
• Public humiliation
• A negative run-in with the law
• Committing a fashion mistake
• Going broke or being frugal
• Offending a person of higher 
renown or social status
REACTIONS
PCs may add their renown 
bonus to their reaction rolls 
when they are in a location 
where they are likely to be 
recognized. Double 1s always 
result in a hostile reaction.

Carousing
These rules are an expansion 
to the Carousing rules from 
Shadowdark RPG pg. 92.
GOING CAROUSING
Characters can go carousing 
as their downtime activity. To 
participate, each PC pitches 
in toward the total cost of the 
event on the below table. 
Then, each participant rolls 1d8 + 
the event's bonus to determine 
their result on the Carousing 
Outcome table. 
NEW BONUSES
PCs can gain bonuses to their 
carousing event rolls due to 
renown (pg. 18), holidays (pg. 
46), bard talents (pg. 12), and 
even their garb or carousing site.
OUTCOME
Each PC gains the XP noted for 
their result, as well as the listed 
number of rolls on the d100 
Carousing Benefit and Mishap 
tables. Add the corresponding % 
Modifier to these d100 rolls.

fluff.full_text:

City Overview
ENVIRONS
The seaside City of Masks, also 
known as Meridia, is hot and 
muggy in the summer, and cool 
and rainy in the winter. Its many 
canals flow into a wide estuary 
where the Trematora River 
meets the ocean. The salty air is 
thick with gulls and mosquitoes.
PEOPLE
Pride and romance burn in 
the hearts of the city's 90,000 
residents. Beggars speak in 
poetry, boat rowers recite epic 
ballads, and even the City Guard 
sings while on patrol.  
But darkness dwells in the city, 
too. Masked conspirators and 
back-alley killers threaten the 
Duke's rule of law at every turn.
TRAVEL IN THE CITY
The city is a highly connected 
maze of bridges, canals, streets, 
and hidden walkways.
PCs move from their current 
location to any destination point 
while traveling in the city. They 
choose their route. It takes 10 
rounds to reach their destination 
point (see City Travel below).
Rush. PCs can rush to reach 
their destination point in 5 
rounds. Increase the random 
encounter chance by 1:6.
Random Encounters. Randomly 
determine which district an 
encounter occurs in if the PCs 
have passed through more than 
one. Shift to crawling or combat 
rounds to play it out.
Destination Point Random Encounter Chance
In same district -
In adjacent district 1:6
In non-adjacent district 2:6
CITY TRAVEL

A bustling  day market that turns into a  night bazaar when the sun  sets. Vendors traditionally wear  black crow feathers in their hats,
fluff.full_text:
41
WORKING DISTRICTS
Major hubs of industry and 
crafting. Ordinary businesses, 
working-class families. Regular 
patrols by the City Guard.
The Rooks (Market). A bustling 
day market that turns into a 
night bazaar when the sun 
sets. Vendors traditionally wear 
black crow feathers in their hats, 
earning them the name "rooks."
Silvertop (Artisan). Named for 
the abundance of jewelers and 
moneychangers in this district. 
Skilled craftworkers, bankers, 
and merchants are found here.
POOR DISTRICTS
Poverty, crowded tenements 
and slums. Crime has a strong 
foothold. Infrequent patrols by 
the City Guard.
Gutterwash (Low). Sewer and 
canal runoff pools here when it 
rains. The stench is part of the 
toilsome life of the resident dock 
workers and hard laborers.
Rilken Row (Slum). Beggars, 
mud, and rickety tenements. 
Crime and misery prevail.
THE CANALS
The bustling canals unite all 
districts by water. Treat any 
district as adjacent on the City 
Travel Table if the characters 
travel to it via the canals (also 
see The Rowers, pg. 44).
WEALTHY DISTRICTS
Strongholds of the arts, politics, 
and religion. Luxury businesses, 
wealthy families. Highly 
patrolled by the City Guard.
Montmar Castle (Castle). The 
Duke's stronghold stands on 
a hill overlooking the city. Fine 
restaurants and bath houses 
cluster outside its walls. 
Gedgarrin (University). Named 
after the wizard's college in this 
district. The Bardic College is 
also here. Libraries, taverns, and 
theaters abound.
Ninestones (Temple). Named for 
the nine dolmens that formed 
the first temple here. Many more 
churches now surround them.
High Harbor (High). The wealthy 
keeps and manor homes here 
look down over the city's canals.

fluff.full_text:
42
Major Factions
BARDIC COLLEGE (L)
A grand academy of high 
archways, sculpted pillars, and 
hazy sunbeams. Music and 
singing fill its airy galleries. 
• Goals. Protect art, truth, and 
enlightenment. Train bards to 
the highest standard so they 
can carry out this mission.
• Structure. Yeothin, Master 
Poet, is the college chancellor. 
He adventured with the Duke 
himself in his youth. Eight 
skilled bards serve as teachers 
alongside 16 administrative 
staff. The college's beloved 
cat, Penny, is actually the 
sphinx, Pendirius, in magical 
disguise. The dorms currently 
house 72 bards-in-training.   
• Enemies. The Shroud 
constantly seeks to entice 
influential bards to its cause.
• Resources. Pendirius has 
protected the college since its 
founding long ago. The school 
is richly funded, and Master 
Yeothin has the Duke's ear.
HOUSE OF SEREN (N)
The Thieves' Guild. It always 
carries the name of the current 
guild master. Long-timers 
simply call it "The House."
• Goals. Grow and take a cut 
from all thieving/mob activity. 
Protect leadership from the 
law at the cost of underlings.
• Structure. Led by Seren, a 
40-year-old human assassin 
of great charm and secrecy. 
She commands 120 thugs, 
60 thieves, 20 elite assassins, 
and countless beggars and 
commoners. She even extorts 
a few corrupt City Guard. Only 
the Duke's forces rival hers. 
• Enemies. The House is always 
at a fragile ceasefire with the 
Duke. Neither can afford (or 
win) an open street war. 
• Resources. The House itself 
is a sprawling, gloomy manor 
with many secrets. Its sizable 
wealth lies scattered (and 
even forgotten) in an ancient, 
subterranean maze of traps.

fluff.snippet: 43 THE SHROUD (C) The ambitious, disaffected, and  power-hungry eventually find  their way into The Shroud. Its  members come from all walks of  life and gather in secret, hiding  their identities behind masks.   • Goals. Enrich themselves  through any means while  keeping their identities secret.
fluff.full_text:
43
THE SHROUD (C)
The ambitious, disaffected, and 
power-hungry eventually find 
their way into The Shroud. Its 
members come from all walks of 
life and gather in secret, hiding 
their identities behind masks.  
• Goals. Enrich themselves 
through any means while 
keeping their identities secret. 
Undermine the Duke and his 
allies. Increase their influence. 
• Structure. All members are 
anonymous and include 
merchants, lords, sorcerers, 
and powerful figures who 
disguise their involvement. A 
council of three Gold Masks 
directs The Shroud. Nine Red 
Masks are their lieutenants, 
and ordinary Masks execute 
street-level activities.   
• Enemies. The Duke and his 
allies. The House of Seren 
often competes for territory 
and criminal opportunity. 
• Resources. Massive secret 
influence and financial 
support. Corrupt merchants, 
magistrates, City Guard, and 
even prominent bards and 
wizards of the city's colleges.
THE DUKE (L)
The Duke Loren di Montmar is 
a 45-year-old knight general. He 
leads with discipline and dignity 
from the castle overlooking the 
city, and ruefully accepts the 
pomp and theater of his station.  
• Goals. Foster a prosperous 
city and loyal subjects. Keep 
his grip on power. Defeat 
those who work against him. 
• Structure. In the city, the 
Duke commands 400 City 
Guard and 80 knights. 12 elite 
knights form his bodyguard, 
and both a high-ranking 
mage and bard from the city's 
colleges counsel him. 50 spies 
serve as the Duke's secret 
service (The Onyx Eye), 12 
magistrates enforce his laws, 
and a court of 30 nobles and 
20 merchants advise him. 
• Enemies. The Shroud works 
tirelessly to weaken the 
Duke's influence, harm his 
allies, and foment unrest.
• Resources. The recent Rat 
Plague strained the treasury; 
the Duke is under pressure to 
accept a strategic marriage in 
order to rebuild the coffers.

Minor Factions
GEDGARRIN (L)
The grey, walled towers of 
Gedgarrin have long stood 
along the shore of the river. The 
mages within are disengaged 
from worldly matters, preferring 
to keep to their arcane studies. 
Archmage Ivanculus, the 
headmaster, only admits true-
hearted students who pass the 
ancient Trial of the Seven Pillars. 
SHE WHO WEEPS (C)
The Cult of the Plague Mother, 
She Who Weeps, festers and 
grows inside the abandoned 
temple of Krull in the Ninestones 
district. Disease has begun to 
spread among beggars and 
workers, and fears of the Rat 
Plague rise anew in the city.
CHARNEL-MEN (N)
Keepers of the dead, grave 
diggers, and cremators. The 
cloaked Charnel-Men are silent, 
grim, and feared. It is said they 
guard the final secrets and 
regrets imparted by the dead.
BEGGARS (N)
They are everywhere. They see 
and hear everything. They are 
ignored. Beggars know more 
than the Duke's secret service. 
They are skeptical of authority 
and wealth and don't part with 
valuable information easily. 
BYWATER BARONS 
(C)
A new group of upstart thugs 
who work out of a ramshackle 
warehouse in Rilken Row. They 
are at odds with The House of 
Seren and have been impinging 
into the Thieves' Guild's territory.
THE ROWERS (L)
Proud boat rowers operate the 
countless small vessels that 
carry goods and passengers 
between the city's docks for 
5 sp a ride. The Rowers recite 
grand ballads and poems as 
they work. A trusted rower can 
come through in a pinch, but 
angering The Rowers can lead to 
a collective ban on their services.

Class: Poor.

7. ASHFALL
Tarry smoke streams day and 
night from the chimneys of 
this ash-streaked keep. Each 
morning, The Charnel-Men 
wheel stinking cartloads of dead 
into the keep's ever-burning 
crematorium. The pensive and 
gloomy Brother Igonus leads 
these 36 black-cloaked cultists 
(N) in their duties, which include 
communing with the dead; The 
Charnel-Men jealously guard 
what they learn from this.
8. THE BILGE POT
Honest folk avoid this dim, swill-
smelling tavern near the docks. 
A dark slurry of mud constantly 
oozes through the floorboards. 
The owner, a sour old cur named 
Shem Turley, buys leftover ale 
from inbound ships and pours 
it into a huge barrel that gives 
the tavern its name. This "bilge" 
is the only drink on offer. The 
Thieves' Guild forms the main 
clientele, but lately, thugs 
connected to the rival Bywater 
Barons (33) have been visiting 
the tavern as a show of force. 
Tensions are fit to burst. Thieves 
and roguish types get a +1 bonus 
to carousing event rolls here.

fluff.full_text:

9. HOUSE OF SEREN
From the exterior, the House of 
Seren (pg. 42) wears the guise 
of an abandoned, two-story 
manor home. Its shutters hang 
askew over lightless windows, 
and the rotted facade sags 
inside a wildly overgrown yard. 
Yet silent, trained panthers slink 
though the jungle-like grounds, 
and assassins and thieves cluster 
in the black shadows that pool 
just beyond the missing front 
door.  Within the foyer, a secret 
panel opens to an opulent 
manse dripping in gems, gold, 
and velvet. Dusty riches sit 
brazenly on display, untouched 
even in this den of thieves, for 
to steal from the House means 
death. Here, killers and rogues 
train in candlelit chambers 
under the expert eye of 
Guildmaster Seren, an assassin 
of surpassing charm and guile. 
As Guildmaster, she alone knows 
that beneath the House are 
fiendishly trapped tunnels filled 
with untold treasures left by her 
forebears. She is convinced that 
the legendary Fingerbone of 
Neem lies within one of these 
lost chambers. Finding it has 
become her obsession. 
10. THE BIRDCAGE
An illegal, after-hours fighting 
ring inside a warehouse. Thugs 
demand the password at the 
door ("fried eggs"). Fights take 
place inside the Birdcage, an 
iron pen. Beating the current 
champ, a half-orc named Rufius 
(orc stats), carries a 50 gp prize.
11. RIVER RATS
The River Rats are a gang of five 
plucky teenage boys who each 
own a peeling, black-painted 
skiff. They're the fastest Rowers 
in the city (it takes 4 rounds 
to arrive at any destination), 
and they charge 3 gp a ride. 
An unhappy customer named 
Mortimer Grund (thief) has been 
spreading lies that the boys have 
contagious Rat Plague. Until this 
rumor stops, anyone seen in a 
River Rats skiff loses 1 renown.
12. SHIELDSTONE LAW
A stooped, fretful barrister 
called Scribald Toderick works 
out of this dim, book-strewn 
office. New clients get 50% off. 
His last client, a thug named 
Porkchop, was hanged for killing 
a noble; Porkchop's friends are 
now out for Scribald's head.

13. THE DUKE'S BRIDGE
The city's most magnificent 
bridge, tall enough for a galleon 
to sail beneath it. It's the main 
thoroughfare for those entering 
the city via the Grand Gate (18). 
Prowling, winged lion statues 
rear along its ramparts; they are 
said to be dormant gargoyles 
that rise up to defend the city in 
its time of need. The city's worst 
criminals famously threaten to 
throw their victims from its lofty 
heights to their deaths.
14. THE ROYAL JEWELER
Humphrey Hammergold, a 
wizened dwarf jeweler of utmost 
skill, runs The Royal Jeweler to 
serve the city's most exclusive 
clientele. Customers must have 
8+ renown to enter; all other 
"garnet gazers" are barred at the 
door by two heavily armed dwarf 
guards (gladiators). Humphrey 
is earnest and obsessed with 
his craft; he can make jewelry 
worth up to 800 gp. He proudly 
displays the most famous garnet 
ever unearthed, The Heart of 
Sidar, a radiant red beauty he 
cut worth 2,000 gp. Wearing 
jewelry made by Humphrey 
grants +1 to carousing event rolls.  
High Harbor District

He hosts lavish  dinners and invites notable
fluff.full_text:

15. VANGLARE HOUSE
An ivy-covered manor with 
a choice, hilltop view of 
Montmar Castle (21). Gaston di 
Vanglare, current patriarch of 
his prominent noble family, is 
in his prime at 60 years thanks 
to a regimen of costly tinctures 
and poultices. He hosts lavish 
dinners and invites notable 
up-and-comers as soon as they 
reach 8 renown. He has a vast 
network of contacts that reaches 
to the Duke himself. Gaston is 
secretly indebted to The Shroud 
for curing his daughter Zara of 
the Rat Plague; cloaked figures 
often visit the house late at night 
and leave just before dawn.
16. ZAMEEK'S CURIOS
Zameek, an energetic halfling 
with an eye for rare finds, buys 
and sells obscure collectibles. 
He is a voracious reader, 
knows everything about lost 
civilizations, and can spot a fake 
from ten miles. His shop smells 
of incense and is full of shelves 
bursting with scrolls, bottles, 
pottery, and trinkets. He recently 
bought a carefully wrapped 
Mirror of Mischief and is trying to 
sort out its exact nature.
17. CLUB LEVANTIS
A swanky, candlelit tavern with 
a faux-seedy vibe (just enough 
to make the wealthy clients 
feel conspiratorial). Handlers 
lead exotic animals around 
on leashes, and skilled bards 
play the latest. Entry requires 
5+ renown, but the back door 
guards accept a 50 gp bribe to 
sneak in as long as you don't 
look like trouble. PCs wearing 
garb worth 200 gp or more get a 
+1 bonus to carousing event rolls 
here. Once a month, PCs have 
ADV on Skulduggery downtime 
checks to start a rumor here.
18. THE GRAND GATE
A pair of towering, golden lion 
statues flank the only land-
based gate into the city. Its 
sturdy gatehouse hosts 30 
elite City Guard. Two younger 
guards, Remy and Ulgrin, have 
unwittingly spiraled into a plot 
with the Thieves' Guild (9) to 
poison the champion racing pig 
Ol' Tangerine (49) during the 
Divine Swine race. They're too 
prideful and terrified to back out 
now, even though they know it's 
wrong. The guilt has made them 
unusually jumpy and gruff.

43) operate out of this heavily

an effective mix of disciplined

27. GRAVEYARD
The city's meandering graveyard 
rises along the southern hills of 
Ninestones. Leaning headstones 
sprout like weeds beside rain-
streaked mausoleums. At the 
center of the graveyard lies the 
baroque Ducal Tomb where the

with a chest stake and copious 
vials of holy water. Clandestine 
lovers and The Shroud often 
meet near this infamous tomb.

Mossy stone walls surround a 
quiet courtyard open to the sky. 
Gnarled trees, grass, and flowers 
grow freely within its borders; 
rabbits dart in the bushes and 
birdsong lilts from the trees. 
An otherworldly peace prevails 
here. An old, cowled woman 
named Mina is always here. She 
is a druid, and though she has 
grown ancient and frail, she 
protects the grove with her life. 
Once a month, neutral PCs have 
ADV on Spiritualism downtime 
checks made here.

The soaring, snow-white 
cathedral of St. Terragnis towers 
high over all other temples and

the enumerable clerics running

Hexcrawl is one of the oldest and most compelling ways to play a 
tabletop RPG. It’s also surprisingly hard to learn from scratch. The 
rules aren’t complex. The problem is that no one has gathered the 
essentials in one place. The best writing on it is scattered across 
decades of blog posts, forum threads, and out-of-print supplements.
When I turned a game designer’s lens on hexcrawl, I found deep 
roots and clear principles, but no practical handbook that lays them 
out in one place. So I wrote one.
This is an opinionated guide. I recommend specific approaches, 
warn you about common failure modes, and tell you what I think 
works best and why, so you can adapt it to your table. Where the 
tradition disagrees with itself, I pick a side and explain why.
Whether you’re running D&D, Shadowdark, 
or anything else with a map and a taste for 
exploration, this book will work. 
System-neutral by design. You can 
read it in an evening and run your 
first hexcrawl next week.
• Matthijs

How Hexcrawl Differs from Other Styles
Hexcrawl gets confused with other exploration-focused styles.
vs. West Marches: West Marches is a social structure: rotating play-
ers, open table, player-initiated sessions. Hexcrawl is a procedural 
structure: hex grid, exploration turns, resource tracking. You can run 
a hexcrawl with a fixed group of four. The overlap is real, but they 
solve different problems.
vs. Pointcrawl: A pointcrawl connects known locations along fixed 
paths. Locations and the connections between them are the focus, 
not the terrain in between. A hexcrawl fills the space between. 
Pointcrawl is efficient. Hexcrawl rewards wandering off the trail.
vs. Traditional Campaigns: In most campaigns, travel is handwaved: 
“three days later, you arrive.” In a hexcrawl, travel IS the adventure. 
The GM shifts from storyteller to world-runner, and the exploration 
turn replaces “skip to the next scene.”
Summary:
• West Marches is a social structure built around an open table.  
 Hexcrawl is a procedural structure built around a hex grid and 
 exploration turns.
• Pointcrawl connects known points. Hexcrawl fills the space 
 between
• Traditional campaigns handwave travel. Hexcrawl makes travel  
 the main event
A Wilderness Waiting to Be Hexplored
The next chapter lays out six principles that define hexcrawl play. To-
gether, they answer the question every new hexcrawl GM asks: 
“Where do I even start?”
The short answer: with a small map, a handful of keyed hexes, and 
the willingness to let your players walk off the edge of your prep.

2. The Hex Grid Structures Everything
Why hexes and not squares? Hexes keep distances honest: 
every neighbor is the same distance away, with no diagonal 
shortcuts. Navigation is intuitive, and measurement is consistent.
In this book I use standard 6-mile hexes (~10 km). You run the explo-
ration turn once per watch, not once per hex. On easy terrain, one 
watch crosses one hex. Moderate terrain (forest, hills) takes two 
watches. Hard terrain (swamp, mountains) takes three. More watches 
per hex means more resource drain and more encounter checks.
For players, distances become easy to read. “The tower is three 
hexes north” means something concrete: about 18 miles.
Summary:
• Hexes beat squares because every neighbor is equidistant, with  
 no diagonal shortcuts
• 6-mile hexes: one watch to cross on clear terrain. “Three hexes  
 north” means 18 miles
• You run the exploration turn once per watch, not once per hex

3. Danger is a Place on the Map
In a hexcrawl, danger is geographic, not random. It’s tied to 
specific hexes and radiates outward from safety in expanding 
rings. The ogre cave doesn’t care that the party is level 2. 
It was there before them and it’ll be there after.
You’re not tuning difficulty to the party. You’re placing threats on 
the map and letting players choose which ones to face.
The world warns players before it kills them. Bigger tracks mean a 
harder zone. Scorched trees mean something breathes fire nearby. 
A fleeing merchant says “don’t go east.” These are spatial warning 
signs. They let players make informed decisions about risk without 
the GM saying “this is too hard for you.”
I recommend sketching three zones expanding from the home base: 
safe (1-2 hexes from base), moderate (3-5 hexes), dangerous (6+). 
This gives you a pacing tool and gives players a visible gradient of risk.
Failure mode: A deadly encounter one hex from base, or uniform dan-
ger everywhere. Both kill the feeling that deeper = more dangerous.
Summary:
• Danger is geographic, in expanding rings from safety, not scaled 
 to party level
• Warning signs (tracks, scorch marks, fleeing NPCs) let players   
 choose their risk
• Sketch three zones from the home base: safe, moderate, dangerous

4. Players See the World Differently Than You Do
You see a numbered hex grid with keyed entries. Players see 
descriptions, landmarks, and the edges of their map. That gap 
between what you know and what they know is central to the 
hexcrawl experience.
Player cartography is a core activity. When a player draws the 
river they just crossed onto their map, they’re engaged at the most 
fundamental level. The map they build over weeks becomes the 
campaign’s most treasured artifact.
Player roles make the exploration turn active for everyone:
• Mapper: fills in the party’s map hex by hex as they explore,   
 recording landmarks and terrain
• Caller: declares the party’s direction and decisions each watch
• Quartermaster: tracks rations, torches, and gear consumption
• Chronicler: writes a short expedition report after each session  
 and maintains the rumor log 
I recommend assigning roles at Session Zero so every player has a 
job from the first watch. Roles can rotate between expeditions, but 
keeping them stable within a session avoids confusion.
Keep the map and notes in a shared location: a photo of the pa-
per map in the group chat, or a shared digital canvas. That way the 
group isn’t stuck if the mapper misses a session.
Failure mode: Players sitting passively, waiting for the GM to tell 
them where to go. That means they don’t have enough information 
to make choices.
Summary:
• You see the grid. Players see descriptions. That gap drives the   
 whole experience
• Player roles (mapper, caller, quartermaster, chronicler) keep 
 everyone active during travel
• Hand out a blank hex grid and colored pencils at Session Zero

5. The GM is a Cartographer, Not a Storyteller
Your main job in a hexcrawl is procedural, not narrative. 
You have four core activities:
Key hexes: Pick some hexes, and write a few sentences per hex
(2-4 is plenty): what’s here, what’s interesting, what’s dangerous
Build encounter tables: One per terrain type. Mix non-combat 
entries (tracks, weather, NPCs, strange sights) with creatures.
For example, a d6 plains table might include: (1) wagon tracks 
leading south, (2) dust storm cuts visibility, (3) circling vultures over 
a dead horse, (4) traveling tinker selling maps and rumor, (5) wild 
horses, skittish but tameable, (6) mounted raiders. Notice: four of 
those six aren’t combat. See chapter 5 for a full breakdown
Track time: Watches, days, rations, seasons. Time creates consequences
Run the exploration turn: Follow the procedure, describe results honestly
A good hex key is short and evocative:“Collapsed watchtower. 
Owlbear nesting in upper floor. Intact cellar with locked iron chest 
(old maps).” That’s enough. Expand at the table if players investigate.
I recommend writing keys per hex, each hex gets its own entry. 
But hexes that share a terrain type can also share an encounter 
table, which saves prep. One page of encounter tables per terrain 
type covers most of what you need.
Failure mode: Steering the party toward “your” content. If they go 
north and you prepped east, let them find what’s north. The con-
tent east will keep.
Summary:
• 4 GM activities: key hexes, build encounter tables, track time,   
 run the turn
• Hex keys should be 2-4 sentences. Expand at the table, not in prep
• One page of hex keys + one page of encounter tables per terrain  
 = 90% of prep

6. Start Small, Expand as They Explore
Your prep is a spotlight centered on the party’s position.
Keying density: In your starting region, key most hexes. Players will 
explore them quickly, and prepared content makes those first ses-
sions sing. As the map grows, the ratio drops.
You don’t need to key hexes the players won’t reach for weeks. Focus 
your prep on hexes along likely routes and at terrain boundaries.
Which hexes to key: Focus on hexes along likely routes and at terrain 
boundaries. A river crossing, a mountain pass, the edge of the forest: 
these are natural decision points where interesting things should live.
How much detail: A few sentences per hex. Write what’s visible, 
what’s hidden, what’s dangerous. Let play fill in the rest. If you’re 
writing more than a paragraph per hex, you’re writing too much. 
Here’s a keyed hex at the right level of detail:
• “Hex 12, Crow Marsh. Knee-deep mud, rotting boardwalk half-  
 submerged. A dead prospector clutches a hand-drawn map show- 
 ing a trail east. Stirges nest in the reeds, attracted by torchlight.”
Four sentences. What you can see, what’s hidden, what’s dangerous. 
That’s enough.
Start with a handful of destinations and a dozen smaller discoveries 
in the region around your home base. Grow outward from there as 
players explore. Chapter 5 defines these categories and shows what 
this looks like in practice.
Failure mode: Keying 200 hexes before session 1. That’s the classic 
burnout trap. Most of those hexes will never be visited.
Summary:
• Key most hexes in the starting region. As the map grows, key fewer
• Start with a handful of destinations and smaller discoveries near 
 the home base
• Trying to key everything before session 1 is the classic burnout trap.

1. Draw Your Hex Map
Start with a hex grid. For paper, search online for “hex grid PDF” 
and print one. For digital, any virtual tabletop with a hex overlay 
works. Don’t overthink the medium. A hand-drawn grid on paper 
is perfectly fine.
Assume the grid uses 6-mile hexes. At that scale, a journey across 3 
hexes on clear terrain fills a full day of travel. A 30-hex map gives 
you weeks of play.
Terrain variety matters more than map size. A 30-hex map with five 
terrain types (forest, hills, swamp, plains, river) creates more inter-
esting decisions than a huge map that’s all forest.
Each terrain type changes travel speed, encounter tables, and sur-
vival conditions, so place at least three types within two days’ travel 
of the home base.
Place natural boundaries: a mountain range that blocks easy pas-
sage, a river that must be forded or bridged, a dark forest that sig-
nals danger. These boundaries create choke points and decision 
points: “do we go around the mountains or risk the pass?”
Summary:
• Start with about 30 hexes at 6 miles each. Terrain variety 
 matters more than size
• Place at least three terrain types within two days of home base
• Natural boundaries (rivers, mountains) create interesting 
 decision points

Major location: A destination players will likely seek out. They’ll 
hear about it through rumors and plan an expedition.
Example: “Hex 07, Iron Tower. Three-story stone tower, partially col-
lapsed. Signs of recent habitation: warm ashes, fresh scratches on 
the inner walls. Locked basement door. Something is living here.”
Minor feature: A discovery players may stumble on while traveling. 
It rewards exploration and connects to other hexes. 
Example: “Hex 02, Pine Barrens. Sparse pines over sandy soil. An 
abandoned camp with a locked chest containing a journal. 
Deer trails, nothing hostile.”
Unkeyed hex: Terrain the players probably won’t reach soon. No 
written entry needed. You know the terrain type from the map, 
and that’s enough. If players enter one, describe the landscape 
and roll on the encounter table.
Notice how short each entry is. Detail grows during play, not during 
prep. The worked example in chapter 6 shows a full 8-hex starting 
region built exactly this way, with encounter tables included.
See chapter 5 for a campaign kickoff checklist that walks you 
through this whole setup process step by step.
Summary:
• Major locations are destinations. Minor features reward 
 exploration. Unkeyed hexes are blank until players go there
• Each tier has a different purpose, but all fit in 2-4 sentences
• See chapter 6 for a worked example of a full starting region

3. Build a Home Base
Every hexcrawl starts with a safe place: a frontier town, a trad-
ing post, a fort on the edge of the wilderness. This is where every 
expedition begins and ends.
Your base should have:
• A name and some flavor, e.g. “Thornwall, a mud-brick town   
 where prospectors drink and argue”
• A few key NPCs: shopkeeper, healer, tavern keeper, rumor source
• A safe haven. The base exists to launch expeditions, not to 
 generate drama
I recommend keeping the base deliberately uninteresting as a 
destination. It’s a workshop, not a theme park. If the base is too 
compelling (political intrigue, NPC drama, side quests in town), 
players will stay there instead of exploring the map.
For players, the base is where they restock, compare notes, and 
plan the next expedition.
Summary:
• Keep the base simple and safe, a workshop, not a destination
• If the base is too interesting, players won’t leave
• The adventure is always out there, not in town

fluff.snippet: 19 4. Seed Rumors and Hooks The map is blank to the players at the start. Rumors are how  they fill it in. I recommend tying each rumor to a specific hex on  your GM map. The players don’t know the number, but you do. Some examples: • “Miners found strange carvings in the canyon walls to the east.”
fluff.full_text:

4. Seed Rumors and Hooks
The map is blank to the players at the start. Rumors are how 
they fill it in. I recommend tying each rumor to a specific hex on 
your GM map. The players don’t know the number, but you do.
Some examples:
• “Miners found strange carvings in the canyon walls to the east.” 
 -> Hex 06
• “A trader says there’s a ruined tower three days north, and   
 strange lights burn in its windows.” -> Hex 07
• “The old hunter claims the swamp past the river shows you visions.” 
 -> Hex 04
Deliver rumors through the world: post them on a quest board, 
spread them as gossip in the marketplace, or have a wounded
adventurer sell a secret at the healer’s. Mix true, partially true,
and misleading.
Failure mode: All rumors pointing in the same direction. If every 
lead says “go east,” you’ve given players one choice disguised as 
several. Spread rumors across the map so the party has genuine 
decisions to make.
Summary:
• Each rumor should point to a specific hex on your GM map
• Mix true, partially true, and misleading. The information game  
 matters
• Spread rumors across the map so players have genuine choices

You look at the map and decide     where to go.” • “The map doesn’t care about your level. Some places will kill you.   Th

5. Invite and Explain the Rules
At your Session Zero, set expectations for hexcrawl play. 
These are the key differences from a typical campaign:
• “There’s no planned route. You look at the map and decide   
 where to go.”
• “The map doesn’t care about your level. Some places will kill you. 
 The greater the risk, the greater the reward.”
• “Rations, torches, and gear are real constraints. You’ll track them.”
• “Travel isn’t downtime between adventures. The journey is the 
 adventure.”
A ready-to-use player handout is included in chapter 5. 
Customize the brackets and hand it out at Session Zero.
Help players build characters suited to the frontier. Anyone who can 
navigate, forage, scout, or survive outdoors will shine. 
Combat specialists are useful but not sufficient. 
The wilderness rewards practical skills more than raw power.
Then assign the four player roles from chapter 1: 
mapper, caller, quartermaster, and chronicler.
Give the mapper a blank hex grid and colored pencils. 
Roles can rotate between sessions.
Summary:
• Explain the core loop: gear up, head out, explore, return
• Assign player roles (mapper, caller, quartermaster, chronicler) 
 so nobody sits idle during travel
• Roles can rotate between sessions. The point is active participation

1. Planning the Session
Session 1 is different. You’ve already prepped the starting region, 
so you’re ready. The first expedition begins at the home base: 
players read the rumor board, pick a direction, and head out. 
No advance planning needed.
Session 2 onward: I recommend having players declare their desti-
nation at least a day before the session. This gives you time to prep 
the right hexes without scrambling.
Ask them:
• Where do you want to go?
• What’s your goal for this trip?
• What route are you planning?
Then prep their route: review key entries, prepare one encounter table 
per terrain type the party might cross (forest, hills, swamp, etc.). These 
are shared across all hexes of that type, saving you from writing tables 
per hex. Note any world changes.
Between-session planning (maps, rumors, debate) means session 
time is spent exploring, not deciding.
Summary:
• Session 1: players pick a rumor and go. You’ve already prepped
• Session 2+: players declare their destination before the session.  
 Prep their likely route.
• They may deviate, but you’ll have the terrain and encounters   
 ready for the area
• Between-session planning (maps, rumors, debate) is part of 
 the game

fluff.full_text:

When an encounter triggers:
• Distance: Are they far away or right on top of you?
• Reaction: Is the creature hostile, curious, or fleeing? Roll 2d6: low 
 = hostile, mid = wary/neutral, high = friendly. If your system lacks  
 one, use this scale.
• Player choice: Do they approach, avoid, or observe?
Not every encounter is a fight. A pack of wolves might be tracking 
prey. A merchant caravan might offer news. A ruined wagon might 
hold clues to a keyed hex nearby.
Failure mode: All-combat encounter tables. If every encounter is a 
fight, the world seems one-dimensional, and players learn to avoid 
travel entirely. Variety turns hexcrawl travel into exploration instead 
of a gauntlet.
Summary:
• Build encounter tables at 60% non-combat, 40% creatures or   
 other potential conflicts
• Use reaction rolls and distance. Not every encounter is a fight
• All-combat tables teach players to avoid travel. Variety keeps   
 them exploring

6. Returning to Base
Expeditions end when the party returns to base. The outbound 
journey is full of unknowns.
That’s where the big decisions live. The return covers familiar 
ground, so you have options:
•  Compress it: One encounter check for the whole journey back,  
 then narrate the arrival. Good for keeping the session moving.
• Show consequences: The party passes through hexes they’ve  
 changed. The bandits they scattered have regrouped. 
 The bridge they damaged is now impassable. The return trip   
 shows what their actions changed.
•  Surprise them: Factions and NPCs don’t stand still. A new camp 
 has appeared on the road. The safe river crossing is now   
 guarded. The world moved while they were away.
Match the approach to the moment. If the session is running long, 
compress. If the players made waves, show what changed.
As the session nears its end:
•  Ask the quartermaster to report how far they are from base and 
 how many rations they have left.
•  If they make it back: they’re safe, time passes, and their discov- 
 eries become part of the world.
•  If they don’t make it back, note where they are. Next session   
 picks up there, and resources keep ticking.
•  Encourage the chronicler to review their notes: what did they  
 find, what’s still out there, what do they want next?
Summary:
•  I suggest compressing the return: one encounter check, 
 then narrate
•  The return is when the expedition report starts forming
•  Smart retreats and early returns are valid play

Frame these as player choices, not GM assignments:  “What does your character do this week?” • Rest and recover: Heal injuries, cure conditions, recover f

1. Downtime Activities
When characters return to base, they can take downtime 
actions (things that happen “off-screen” between expeditions). 
Frame these as player choices, not GM assignments: 
“What does your character do this week?”
• Rest and recover: Heal injuries, cure conditions, recover from 
 exhaustion
• Resupply: Buy rations, torches, rope, special gear for the next trip
• Research: Ask around about ruins, creatures, or a region they   
 plan to visit
• Hire help: Pay for guides, porters, or guards
• Contribute to the base: Fund a new shop, build a stable, sponsor  
 a scout post. Every investment should make the next expedition  
 easier or open new routes.
For example: “Aldric spends the week asking about the dwarven 
symbols from the cave. The scholar says they mark a tomb en-
trance, and that the dwarves trapped their tombs.”
That’s one downtime action that gives the party actionable infor-
mation for their next expedition. A good rule of thumb: each char-
acter can complete one downtime task per week. Players can stay 
longer, but remind them that the world outside the gates keeps 
moving. Factions advance, weather shifts, and opportunities expire. 
The adventure is out there.
Summary:
• Frame downtime as player choices: “What does your character  
 do this week?”
• Downtime actions can yield new rumors, gear, or advantages
• Connect downtime results to the next expedition whenever possible

A faction is any group with a name and an agenda. You probably  won’t need factions until a few sessions in, when the players have  made enough noise to attr

4. Factions and the Living World
The wilderness shouldn’t stand still while the players are in town. 
Factions make the hex map feel alive.
A faction is any group with a name and an agenda. You probably 
won’t need factions until a few sessions in, when the players have 
made enough noise to attract attention. When you do, keep a short 
list. For each faction, note three things: who they are, what they want, 
and one or two key figures the players might meet. For example:
• Goblins of Hex 03 (want to expand territory).
 Leader: Skrag, a cunning scout.
• Iron Road Merchants (want safe trade routes).
 Contact: Dalla, a caravan boss who pays for information.
• The Displaced Bandits (want revenge on the party).
 Leader: Harsk, a scarred veteran the players will recognize.

fluff.full_text:

Between sessions, ask yourself: “What has changed?” 
Pick one or two things:
• The goblins have moved from Hex 03 to Hex 05, and the bridge  
 crossing is now guarded
• The Iron Road Merchants have established a camp at Hex 04,  
 bringing new rumors and trade
• The bandits the party drove off have regrouped two hexes 
 further east
As factions grow important, add them to your encounter tables. If 
the goblins control Hex 05, they should show up on that hex’s 
encounter rolls.
Failure mode: Factions that only exist in hexes the players haven’t 
been to yet. If changes never touch explored territory, they’re invisible.
This gives you everything you need to run factions. Once you’ve 
played a campaign or two, the Encounter Design Guidebook has 
more techniques for weaving factions into your encounter tables.
Summary:
• A faction needs three things: a name, an agenda, and a key figure
• Between sessions, ask “what has changed?” and update 1-2 factions
• Add important factions to encounter tables so players meet   
 them on the road

5. Time Keeps Moving
I recommend a default of 1 week of in-game time between 
sessions. This creates natural consequences without overwhelm-
ing bookkeeping.
That means:
• Seasons change, affecting travel speed and survival conditions
• Rumors grow old or are overtaken by events
• Enemies regroup, fortify, or move on
• New threats emerge, especially if left unchecked
Start each session with a brief update: 
“A week has passed. The first snow has fallen on the ridge. A new 
merchant arrived in Thornwall.”
This signals that the world doesn’t 
pause for them.
A loose week count 
is enough.
Summary:
• Default to 1 week of in-  
 game time between 
 sessions
• Start each session with a  
 brief “what’s changed”   
 update
• Time passing creates 
 urgency. Leads don’t   
 wait forever

1. Essential Tools
You need three tools for Session Zero:
• Hex map with terrain types filled in (hand-drawn or digital)
• Hex key document: numbered entries, 2-4 sentences each
• Encounter tables: one per terrain type, d6 is enough to start
Once you’re running, add these as needed:
• Blank hex grid: for player mapping (physical or digital)
• Session log: A few bullet points after each game: where the   
 party went, what they found, what they left unfinished. 
 The chronicler (chapter 1) keeps the player version. You keep   
 your own, including things the players don’t know yet.
• Rumor tracker: A simple table with three columns: the rumor,  
 where it came from, and its status. You don’t need to decide   
 whether a rumor is true when you write it. Let play settle that.
Rumor Source Status
“Something shines in the 
eastern ravine at dawn”
Tavern keeper, 
session 2 Investigating
“The Iron Tower is cursed, 
no one returns”
Traveling merchant, 
session 3 Unverified
“Goblins are afraid of the 
standing stones”
Captured goblin, 
session 4 Confirmed
• World clock: A numbered list of in-game weeks. After each 
 session, note what changed in the world: factions moved, 
 seasons shifted, threats grew. This doesn’t need to be detailed. It  
 just keeps time feeling real. For example:
Week What changed
1 Goblins spotted near the bridge.
2 Merchant caravan arrives at Thornwall. First frost, swamp partially freezes.
3 Party rests in Thornwall. Ranger forages, thief ask around about the tower.
4 Goblins now control bridge crossing. Bandits regroup east of the river

3. Session Prep Checklist
Session prep should take 30-60 minutes. If you’re spending 3+ 
hours, you might be over-keying, or you might just love world-
building. Either way, most of that detail won’t hit the table this 
session. Prep what’s on the party’s route and save the rest.
Before Prep:
• Get the players’ destination and route (before the session)
• Identify the hexes along their likely path
Prepare:
• Key unkeyed hexes on their route and prepare 2-3 encounters  
 per terrain type
• Any NPCs or creatures at their destination
• Weather and travel conditions
• Review rumors and previous discoveries
• 1-2 world changes since last session (factions, weather, events)
That’s it. Let the players fill in the rest with their choices.
Failure mode: Prepping everything the players might do. Prep what 
they said they’ll do. If they change course mid-session, improvise or 
use your encounter tables

5. Sample Player-Facing Document
Hand this out at Session Zero. Customize the [brackets] for your game.
“Welcome to the Hexcrawl!
You’ll explore unknown territory, discover ruins, map the frontier, 
and manage your supplies.
How it works:
• You decide where to go. Check the rumor board, review your   
 map, and pick a destination.
• The wilderness is not balanced. Some areas are deadly. Watch  
 for warning signs.
• Resources matter. Track rations, torches, and gear. Running out  
 is dangerous.
• Not every fight is winnable. Retreating is smart play, not failure.
• The world changes between sessions based on what you do   
 (and don’t do).
Player roles (rotate each session):
• Mapper: Draw the party’s map as you explore.
• Caller: Declare the party’s direction each watch.
• Quartermaster: Track rations, torches, and gear.
• Chronicler: Write a short expedition report after each session   
 and maintain the rumor log.
To start: Make a character using [RULESET]. Check the rumor 
board. Pick a direction. Head out.”

8. When Players Arrive Somewhere Strange
The exploration turn gets the party to a new place. Now what? 
A crumbling tower, a fungal grove, a camp of lizardfolk traders. 
The hex key says what’s here. Your job is to make the players 
want to interact with it.
I recommend leading with a sensory detail, not a threat. 
“The air smells like wet copper and something is singing under-
ground” does more work than “you see a cave entrance.”
The first invites questions. The second invites caution. Start with 
something that makes players curious, not defensive.
Give every creature or NPC a visible motivation. 
The ogre is dragging a dead elk toward its lair. The hermit is repair-
ing a collapsed wall and cursing. The fungal guardians pulse 
brighter when you step closer to the spore pool.
Motivation is what turns a stat block into a scene. Players can’t role-
play with “hostile creature blocks your path.” They can roleplay with 
“it’s protecting something.”
Offer three ways in: When the party arrives at a location with in-
habitants, frame three approaches:
• Talk: Who here would speak to outsiders, and what do they want?
• Trade: What do they have that the party needs, and vice versa? 
• Observe: What can the party learn by watching before engaging?
Not every location supports all three. A territorial beast has no one 
to talk to, but you can still observe it and figure out what it’s guard-
ing. A ghost might talk but can’t trade. The point is: combat is one 
option among several, and the GM should signal the others.

1. Worked Example: The Thornwall Frontier
Here are 7 keyed hexes and 1 unkeyed hex showing what a start-
ing region actually looks like. This is enough to run 2-3 sessions.
Hex 01, Thornwall (home base). Mud-brick town on a bluff. Market 
square, the Antler & Axe tavern, Marta the healer. Prospectors drink 
and argue about what’s in the hills. Rumor board by the gate.
Hex 02, Pine Barrens (minor feature). Sparse pines over sandy soil. 
An abandoned camp with a locked chest containing a journal. Entries 
describe “something shining” in Hex 06. Deer trails, nothing hostile.
Hex 03, Winding River (minor feature). Collapsed stone bridge, 
waist-deep ford. A submerged merchant wagon holds 30gp in trade 
goods. Giant crayfish (2) nest under the bridge rubble, territorial, not 
aggressive unless disturbed.
Hex 04, Fog Hollow (minor feature). Standing stones in ankle-
deep water. Touching the central stone triggers a vision: a dark 
tower against red sky (Hex 07). Leeches drain 1 ration equivalent 
per watch spent here. Eerie, no combat.
Hex 05, Rocky Ridge (minor feature). High ground with long 
views. From the summit, players can see smoke from Thornwall, 
the river, and the dark tree line to the east. Good camp spot. 
Sheltered from weather.
Hex 06, Bone Pit (major location). Ancient fossils exposed in the 
cliff face. Giant bats roost in an overhang. Copper ore vein (valuable 
if mined). A narrow tunnel leads deeper, unkeyed, left for the GM to 
develop later.
Hex 07, Iron Tower (major location). A session-sized adventure 
site. Three-story stone tower, partially collapsed. Signs of recent 
habitation (warm ashes, fresh scratches). Locked basement door. 
Whatever is inside is left for you to decide.
Hex 08, Dark Pine Ridge (unkeyed). Dense forest, no trail. Roll on 
the forest encounter table.
Notice the variety: safe base, minor discoveries, clues pointing for-
ward, a hazard, scenic high ground, a full adventure site, and blank 
forest that’s just terrain until players make it more.

Final Thoughts
You now have everything you need to run 
your first hexcrawl and run it well.
The most common mistake I see is waiting 
too long to start. You don’t need 200 keyed 
hexes or custom encounter tables for every 
biome. You need a small starting region 
(around 20-30 hexes), a dozen keyed loca-
tions, a d6 encounter table, and five rumors.
Draw the map tonight. Key a few hexes. 
Write the rumors. Invite your friends.
The wilderness is waiting.
The first time a player draws a river onto 
their map and asks “what’s on the other 
side?”, you’ll know why you started.

fluff.full_text:
This book gave you the foundation: the exploration turn, 
the hex map, the session loop. You can run a great hexcrawl 
with nothing else. But if you want to go deeper, the rest of 
the series is built to snap onto what you already know.
The Encounter Design Guidebook is your next step if your 
encounter tables feel thin. It covers the four encounter cate-
gories (creatures, signs, hazards and discoveries), terrain-
specific tables, faction presence in your rolls, slow threats 
that build across watches, and pacing techniques that 
make travel feel like a journey instead of a series of interrup-
tions. If you've run a few sessions and want your random 
encounters to carry more weight, start here.
The Worldbuilding Guidebook is for when your map needs 
more depth. It walks you through building terrain that 
shapes play, keying hexes at different densities, designing 
factions with territory and agendas, and layering history into 
your landscape so every ruin tells a story. If you're expanding 
beyond your starting region or building a second campaign 
from scratch, this is where the craft lives
Each book shares the same voice, the same format, and 
the same assumption: you're a busy GM who wants practical 
tools, not theory. Pick the one that solves the problem you have 
right now.

WHAT ARE THE 
WESTERN REACHES?
The Western Reaches are a 
place of dangerous fantasy 
adventuring where heroes can 
strike out to explore the land, 
find incredible treasures, and 
make a name for themselves.
This official Shadowdark RPG 
setting combines all the world 
building material from Cursed 
Scroll zines 1-6 (CS 1-6) into a 
regional setting that can be 
traversed from top to bottom.
The Player's Guide to the 
Western Reaches (PGWR) works 
with the Game Master's Guide 
to the Western Reaches (GMWR) 
to outline what players and GMs 
need to know to run and play in 
games in the Reaches.
If you're a player, you'll want to 
avoid the spoilers in the GMWR. 
This book is all you need — it 
will orient you to the Western 
Reaches and help you build a 
character ready to explore them!
HOW DO I PLAY IN 
THIS SETTING?
Check out the Overview chapter 
first (pg. 11) to learn some 
everyday knowledge about the 
Western Reaches.
You as the player will know 
what a typical character in the 
Western Reaches knows about 
the world. That is, not much!
The Reaches are meant to be 
explored and discovered using 
sandbox style gameplay. That 
means the Game Master will 
supply you and your adventuring 
party with rumors, leads, and 
mysteries. But it's up to you to 
decide which threads to pull.
In the Reaches, your fate is in 
your own hands. Will your story 
eventually become a legend? 
The later chapters of this book 
contain character building rules. 
You can also use the official, 
free Shadowdark RPG character 
builder, shadowdarklings.net!

What Everyone Knows
Ten things (which may not even 
be true) everyone knows about 
the Western Reaches.
1. The Reaches are ancient. 
They've been here since the sun 
first rose over the western shore. 
Some say the land came up out 
of the sea, or the gods sculpted 
it all out of clay, or the dwarves 
hammered it together on anvils. 
Nobody really knows. But there's 
plenty of old stuff all around that 
must have been built ages ago. 
2. There are faraway lands. 
They say the Reaches stretch all 
the way up to a frozen land of 
endless night, and all the way 
down to deserts so hot they'll 
cook you alive. There's even a big 
city on the coast. City of Masks, 
they call it. Most people don't 
travel too far, though. Too risky. 
3. It's dangerous out there. 
Nobody's going to come riding 
to your rescue! These are lawless 
lands full of bandits and thieves. 
Wild beasts and trolls. Evil spirits. 
You'd better not go alone.
4. The world ends at the Last 
Sea. There's nothing else west 
of the coast. Just the Last Sea 
rolling on and on into mist. 
Some say if you keep going, 
you'll eventually arrive at the 
shores of the gods' realm and 
you can ask them for one thing. 
But you'd never make it back 
from there anyhow. 
5. No king has ever ruled all the 
Reaches. Sure, some have tried. 
But the Reaches have no king, 
not now, not ever. There was 
a queen long ago who almost 
conquered it all from top to 
bottom, but her heart was dark 
and the gods cast her down. 
Every child knows the song: Rise 
and fight, sun from night, dark 
queen tumbles out of sight. 
6. The gods are distant. The 
gods don't walk among us 
anymore. And they don't 
intervene. There are a few 
rare folks like priests who can 
channel their power. That's how 
we know they're still watching 
over us, for good or for ill.

You've heard of the Willowman  who comes to scare children  who don't listen. He's real! And  there are other things like him. 8. Magic is terribly dangerous.  Most folks don'

7. Ancient spirits and beings 
dwell here. There's all kinds of 
strange demons and ghosts 
lurking around in the wilds. 
You've heard of the Willowman 
who comes to scare children 
who don't listen. He's real! And 
there are other things like him.
8. Magic is terribly dangerous. 
Most folks don't trust a wizard, 
I'll tell you that. Only a madman 
lets a wizard cast a spell in his 
house. You'll get yourself blown 
up that way. Even touching a 
magic sword has half a chance 
of cursing you blind!
9. Non-humans aren't very 
common.  Elves, dwarves, you 
don't often see them. We do 
get a traveler from time to time, 
and the kids always want to ask 
them a barrel of questions. 
10. Most of the Reaches are 
unexplored. You'll hear a couple 
tall tales from sailors, but most 
folks haven't seen much farther 
than the ends of their own 
noses. Hard to believe half the 
stuff those sailors say, anyway. 
None of them have even been to 
the south. Can't sail a boat over 
the desert, can you?

If they live in a city-state or  its nearby lands, they pledge  loyalty to its overlord and serve  as vassals in exchange for the  overlord's protection. In most parts of the Rea
fluff.full_text:
15
SOCIAL STRUCTURE
Most people in the Western 
Reaches come from humble 
means and get by working in a 
trade or craft. 
If they live in a city-state or 
its nearby lands, they pledge 
loyalty to its overlord and serve 
as vassals in exchange for the 
overlord's protection.
In most parts of the Reaches, 
there is no overlord. Many towns 
and villages have no other 
authority than their own and 
must protect themselves from 
outside dangers. 
There is no universal set of laws, 
governance, or culture across 
the Western Reaches.
A knight from the Duchy 
of Montmar would not be 
recognized or treated as a noble 
by the lawless bandit lords who 
roam the Djurum Desert. 
A visitor in the City of Masks 
might unknowingly break one 
of the Duke's laws. In Alkesh, 
the very same "crime" might be 
perfectly legal, or perhaps it is 
punished even more harshly.
CIVILIZATIONS
Most people who dwell in the 
Western Reaches have at least 
heard of the other centers of 
power in the region and know a 
few facts about them.
City of Masks. The Duke reigns 
over this romantic city of high 
culture, art, and danger. It's 
the biggest city-state in all the 
Western Reaches. 
Alkesh. A princess called the 
Shar rules Alkesh. The city is 
a mysterious, bright oasis in 
the desert where you can buy 
anything for the right price. 
Stonehall. A dwarf king as old 
as three men presides over a 
vast hall under the mountains. 
The dwarves of Stonehall are the 
best crafters in all the land.
Kyzian Steppes. Wild tribes of 
horseback riders roam across 
the plains like a moving army. 
Their queen is a feared warrior.
Lydonia. An aloof elf king rules 
over a shining citadel deep 
in the forest. His rangers and 
knights watch from behind 
every tree and blade of grass.

The Bards
The Bards is a lawful faction that 
fights for knowledge and justice.  
Their symbol is a gold pendant 
of a nine-pointed star, often 
referred to as The Duke's Rose.
The faction is led by the 
honorable and wise Master Poet 
Yeothin, chancellor of the Bardic 
College in the City of Masks. 
MISSION
To preserve important 
knowledge and prevent the rise 
of evil in the Western Reaches. 
BYLAWS
1. Do not allow evil to stand 
uncontested.
2. Bring light and hope to the 
weak and defenseless.
3. Seek artifacts, knowledge, and 
experience so it may be kept 
safe in your hands.
IN THE REACHES
The Bards operate out of the 
City of Masks, but they travel 
far around the Reaches in small 
groups. People greet bards with 
joy and, often, requests for help.
Typical members include bards, 
fighters, lawful priests, and those 
with strong moral fiber. 
Members in good standing learn 
a mix of rumors about evil plots, 
magic items , and people who 
need help.
